Summary

Productive is an operations system for agencies, consultancies and other professional services firms, joining project delivery to the money side: budgets, time, resourcing, invoicing and a sales pipeline. It suits firms of tens to hundreds of people that bill clients for time.

Projects hold task lists with boards, lists, tables, a calendar of due dates, sprints and, from Professional, a Gantt layout with dependencies. Every task, time entry and booking hangs off a budget and a service, which is what makes profitability reports, forecasting and the Scenario Builder possible, and also what makes the first setup heavier than a task tool.

Essential costs $10 per user per month billed annually ($12 monthly), with a three-seat minimum, and already includes time tracking, resource planning, expenses, docs, the API and an AI assistant with a monthly usage allowance. Professional at $25 adds the Gantt layout, approvals, rate cards and saved views; revenue forecasting, multiple subsidiaries, enforced SSO and webhooks are on Ultimate.

Data sits on AWS in the EU under a SOC 2 Type II report and a DPA with Standard Contractual Clauses. AI runs on OpenAI, Anthropic and Google models, with a stated commitment that neither Productive nor its providers train on customer data. Exports are per table, so leaving at scale means the API.

Summary

Redbooth is a long-running team task manager, launched as Teambox in Barcelona and renamed in 2014. It is aimed at small and mid-sized teams such as agencies, construction firms and higher-education marketing groups that want tasks, discussion and video calls in one place.

Work sits in workspaces holding task lists, conversations, notes and files. Tasks can be viewed on a Kanban board, a timeline with finish-to-start dependencies, a team calendar or a cross-workspace overview, and Zoom-powered HD meetings start from a task. Workspace templates, web forms and public links (added in October 2026) round it out; custom fields and built-in automation rules are not documented.

The free plan stops at two users and two workspaces. Pro at $9 per user per month (annual) adds dependencies, time tracking, SAML SSO, video calls and the MCP server; Business at $15 adds reports, swimlanes, time estimates and Redbooth AI, which trims titles, suggests subtasks and summarises comment threads.

Data is on AWS in a region the vendor does not name, with no residency choice; the security page still cites Privacy Shield, and neither the terms nor the DPA names a legal entity. The AI provider and training policy are not stated. Leaving is realistic: admins can generate a ZIP of JSON files with every task, comment and conversation.

Free stops at two users; Pro at $9 a user adds dependencies, time tracking and SSO without a seat minimum.
Ease of use4.0
Workspaces, task lists and a board view that a new team can use the same day.
Enterprise features2.8
SAML SSO from Pro and multi-organisation settings on Enterprise, but no SCIM, audit log or certification of its own.
Interface flexibility3.6
Kanban, timeline, calendar and overview views with templates, web forms and reports; no custom fields or automation rules documented.
Data control2.0
AWS hosting in an unnamed region with no residency choice, and a security page still citing Privacy Shield.
Portability3.8
Admins download every task, comment and conversation as JSON, plus an OAuth API, but importers are copy and paste.

Web, iOS and Android, plus a Chrome extension and Gmail and Outlook add-ins.

Summary

Shortcut, called Clubhouse until 2021, organises software work as stories grouped into epics, timed into iterations and tied to objectives. It is sold to product and engineering teams that want sprints and a roadmap without Jira’s administration.

Stories move across Kanban boards through custom workflows; a backlog, a roadmap with table and timeline layouts, built-in docs and reports for velocity, cycle time and cumulative flow sit alongside. The roadmap timeline draws no dependencies, there is no calendar view and no time tracking. Korey, an AI agent launched in September 2025, drafts specs and stories and hands work to coding agents.

The free plan covers 10 users with one team and one workflow. Team at $8.50 a seat (yearly) adds automations, WIP limits, five workflows and the calendar feed; Business at $12 adds unlimited teams, objectives and key results, advanced custom fields and extra workspaces. SSO costs extra until Enterprise.

Data sits on AWS with SOC 2 Type II audits and backups every 10 minutes; there is no region choice. Korey is priced per organisation, and Shortcut says Korey inputs and outputs are not used for training. Leaving means CSV story exports or the API, with importers in from Jira, Trello, Linear and Pivotal Tracker.

Ten free users with sprints and a roadmap, then $8.50 a seat; custom fields and objectives wait for $12 Business.

Stories, epics and iterations map directly onto how software teams already talk, and the board needs little setup.
Enterprise features2.8

Interface flexibility3.3
Boards, backlog, roadmap table and timeline, docs, burndown and cycle-time reports and custom workflows, but no calendar view.
Data control2.8
SOC 2 Type II and a HIPAA BAA, but one AWS hosting location with no residency choice and no self-managed edition.
Portability3.3
Story CSVs leave out comments, but the REST API is open on every plan and importers cover Jira, Trello, Linear and Pivotal.

Summary

Sunsama is a daily planner for knowledge workers who want each morning to start with a deliberate plan. It is sold per person, with a shared-workspace option for teams who want one bill.

The core object is a task placed on a day. A board of day columns sits beside your real calendar, and you drag tasks into time slots that write back to Google, Outlook or iCloud. Integrations pull issues, cards and emails in from Jira, Asana, Linear, Gmail and about 20 other tools. There are channels, weekly objectives and a timer, but no projects in the usual sense, no custom fields and no Gantt.

There is one self-serve plan, Pro, at $17 a month billed annually or $22 monthly, and no free tier. That single plan replaced a short-lived split into Basic Pro and Power Pro in spring 2026, and it still makes Sunsama one of the dearest per-seat tools in this comparison for a single person.

All data is stored in the United States on Google Cloud, MongoDB Atlas and AWS. SOC 2 Type II arrived in late 2025, and SSO, SCIM and audit logs sit on a quote-only Enterprise tier. The AI assistant, Sunny, and the MCP server are on Pro, and the privacy policy says customer data never trains models. Leaving relies on a whole-history export, since there is no public API.

No free plan and $17 to $22 a month per person, more than most team tools charge for a single seat.

Summary

Superlist is a to-do list app from the people who built Wunderlist, rebuilt after Microsoft closed that app. It is aimed at individuals and small groups who share household or project lists, with AI capture added on top.

A list is a document: tasks sit beside text, headers and images, and each task opens into its own page of subtasks, notes and attachments. Lists can be shared with assignees and comments. Meeting notes and voice input turn speech into tasks. There is no board, calendar view, time tracking or Gantt.

The free plan stops at five private and five shared lists. Basic, at $59 a year or $6 a month, removes those limits and opens the integrations, while Super at $249 a year is for heavy AI meeting-note use. Teams pay the same per-member rate.

The privacy policy names Hetzner in Germany for hosting, alongside US processors, and Google Gemini, OpenAI and Deepgram for AI features; it does not say whether those providers may train on your data. A CSV export of the whole account arrived in January 2026, and an MCP server in May 2026, but there is no public API.

TeamGantt Drag-and-drop Gantt scheduling for small teams and builders, priced per account and per project rather than per seat.
TeamsTeamGantt 2009 Medium ≈$4.91†$49 flatFree plan 5-15 3.0Mean of the six criteria: 3.0 out of 5

TeamGantt - summary, assessment and sources

Capabilities

TimeTime tracking: Native.
BoardsKanban or Scrum boards: Native.
GanttGantt or dependency timeline: Native.
CalCalendar view: Native.
SyncA one-way iCal feed of assigned tasks and milestones, or chosen projects, for Google Calendar, Outlook or Apple Calendar.Two-way calendar sync: Partial. A one-way iCal feed of assigned tasks and milestones, or chosen projects, for Google Calendar, Outlook or Apple Calendar.

Summary

TeamGantt is a Gantt chart scheduler that started in 2009 as a tool for a Baltimore roofing contractor, and it has gone back to those roots: its pages now speak mostly to home builders, remodelers and trade contractors, though any small team can use it.

A project is a Gantt chart with groups, tasks, milestones and dependencies, with critical path on every plan; list and calendar views come everywhere, while Kanban, workload, time tracking, portfolios and advanced dependencies start at Business. Builder Edition adds lookahead schedules, material lead times and a Procore sync. Custom workflows are reserved for Builder Edition, and other automation runs through Zapier.

Pricing is by account and project rather than seat. Base is $589 a year for 1 manager, 10 collaborators and 5 projects of up to 150 tasks; Business is $1,140 a year with unlimited people and 5 projects, then $24 a month per project up to 20. Trials need a card.

Data is stored in the United States on AWS with nightly backups; TeamGantt publishes no certifications, no DPA and nothing on how its AI project creation handles data. Leaving is easier: each project exports to CSV, PDF or MS Project, and the REST API covers tasks, time, comments and files.

Assessment

Value for money3.0
No per-seat bill, but Base caps at five projects and Business charges $24 a month for each project beyond five.
Ease of use4.4
Drag-and-drop bars and dependencies on one Gantt screen, and collaborators can only update progress, not reshape the plan.
Enterprise features2.0
SSO only on the quoted Enterprise plan, no published certifications and a simple manager and collaborator model.
Interface flexibility3.0
Gantt, list, calendar and Kanban views with workload and portfolio views; custom workflows only in Builder Edition.
Data control1.5
US-only hosting on AWS, no certifications and a privacy policy that never mentions a DPA or AI.
Portability3.8
Any project exports to CSV, PDF or MS Project format, and the REST API reaches tasks, time, comments and documents.

Record

First launched
2009. Year TeamGantt was founded and first built; the vendor does not date the first public release separately.
Vendor
TeamGantt. Bootstrapped and privately held, never taken outside equity; headquartered in Baltimore, Maryland, US, with a fully remote team of 22.
Website
teamgantt.com
Plans
Personal free; Base $59 a month or $589 a year; Business from $120 a month or $1,140 a year with 5 projects, plus $24 a month per extra project up to 20; Builder Edition from $199 a month or $1,908 a year; Enterprise by quote.
Free plan
TeamGantt Personal is free for 1 user, 1 project and 40 tasks with basic Gantt features and dependencies; anything shared needs a paid plan.
Hosting
Amazon Web Services; the privacy policy says personal information is stored in the United States. No region choice and no self-managed edition.
Security
SSL in transit, encrypted passwords, uploaded files served only through an authenticated script, two nightly backups. No SOC 2 or ISO 27001 published; SSO only on Enterprise.
Calendar sync
One-way iCal feed of your assigned tasks and milestones, or of selected projects, subscribed by URL in Google Calendar, Outlook or Apple Calendar; Google refreshes every few hours.
Data out
Export any project to CSV, PDF or Microsoft Project format on all paid plans. Public REST API (api.teamgantt.com/v1) covering projects, tasks, time blocks, comments, documents, custom fields and webhooks. Imports from MS Project .mpp, Primavera P6 and CSV.
Platforms
Web on Mac and PC; iOS and Android apps.
AI
AI project creation on all paid plans and a free AI Gantt chart maker on the website; the privacy policy names no AI provider and says nothing on training.
Integrations
Procore, Trello, Slack, Dropbox, Basecamp 2 and Zapier, plus an iCal feed and imports from MS Project, Primavera P6 and CSV; a public REST API with token auth and webhooks.
Market signal
TeamGantt cites 2M+ users in 120 countries over its life, 20,000+ teams and a staff of 22 (teamgantt.com, about and pricing pages, November 2026).
Caveat
Pricing is now a flat account fee with project caps (pricing page republished in September 2026), not the per-manager seats TeamGantt used to sell, so older comparisons quote the wrong model.
Confidence
High

Teamhood Project and resource planning on boards, lists, Gantt and schedules, aimed at engineering and architecture firms. One paid plan, EU-hosted.
TeamsEylean 2020 Medium ≈$12†$12No free plan 5-10 3.6Mean of the six criteria: 3.6 out of 5

Teamhood - summary, assessment and sources

Capabilities

TimeTime tracking: Native.
BoardsKanban or Scrum boards: Native.
GanttGantt or dependency timeline: Native.
CalCalendar view: Not native.
SyncTwo-way calendar sync: Not native.

Summary

Teamhood is a project planning service from a Lithuanian company that now sells mainly to engineering, architecture and other technical firms running many projects with the same people. Its pitch is resource planning: showing each person’s planned hours across every project so overbooking is visible.

Work is built from configurable item types and fields, shown in list, board, Gantt, schedule, mind map, timesheet and chart views. The Gantt reschedules dependent items, keeps baselines and previews what a change will move; the schedule view becomes a capacity plan when grouped by person. There is no calendar view, no calendar sync and no mobile app.

The current product has one paid plan at $12 (€11) per user per month billed annually, with a three-licence minimum and guests counted as members. There is no free plan, only a one-month trial. Enterprise is quote-only. Customers of the earlier Teamhood Classic keep its separate four-plan structure.

Data sits on Microsoft Azure in the EU; Enterprise can choose Germany or the US, or run dedicated, hybrid or on-premise installations. Teamhood holds no ISO 27001 or SOC 2 of its own. The Chat assistant uses OpenAI with stored responses off. List views export to Excel and CSV and the REST API reads everything, but only while the subscription is paid.

Assessment

Value for money2.8
No free plan and a three-licence minimum at $12, though API, AI chat and resource planning are all included.
Ease of use3.1
Configurable item types, fields and roles suit planners, but a new team has setup to do before it works.
Enterprise features3.3
Custom roles, portfolio views and forced two-factor sign-in; SSO and SCIM only on quote-based Enterprise, and no own certification.
Interface flexibility4.0
List, board, Gantt, schedule, mind map, timesheet and chart views with formula fields, templates and rollups, but no calendar.
Data control4.5
EU Azure hosting by default, with Enterprise choices of Germany, US, dedicated, hybrid or on-premise installation.
Portability4.0
Excel and CSV export from list views and a full REST API, but a lapsed organisation cannot read its own data.

Record

First launched
2020. Approximate: a 2024 vendor blog post says the first Teamhood version went live four years and 100 releases earlier, and a May 2021 press release already describes an upgrade of the platform; Eylean itself dates from 2011.
Vendor
UAB Eylean, Vilnius, Lithuania. Privately held; makers of Eylean Board since 2011, with Vidas Vasiliauskas as CEO.
Website
teamhood.com
Plans
Teamhood $12 (€11) per user per month billed annually or $16 (€14) monthly, minimum 3 licences; Enterprise is quote-only and adds SSO, SCIM, invoice billing and dedicated, hybrid or on-premise hosting. Existing customers on Teamhood Classic keep its Personal (free), Team, Business and Enterprise plans.
Free plan
No free plan: the first month is a free trial without a card, after which every member, open invite and guest needs a paid licence.
Hosting
Microsoft Azure in the EU with failover to another EU region; Enterprise can pick the EU, Germany or the US, or dedicated, hybrid (database on the customer’s servers) or on-premise hosting with customer-installed updates.
Security
Teamhood states it holds neither ISO 27001 nor SOC 2 (Azure does); TLS in transit, encryption at rest, hourly backups with 7-day point-in-time restore, organisation-wide 2FA on every plan; SSO and SCIM on Enterprise; a DPA from UAB Eylean lists subprocessors.
Calendar sync
None documented: no Google or Outlook sync and no iCal feed.
Data out
List views export visible columns to Excel or CSV; timesheets export with cost; Gantt downloads as PDF; a REST API (200 requests a minute per organisation) and webhooks read everything, including per-item history. A lapsed organisation is closed and cannot export until renewed.
Platforms
Web only; the vendor states there are no mobile apps.
AI
In-app Chat on every licence uses OpenAI with stored responses turned off; OpenAI keeps API data up to 30 days for abuse checks and does not train on it. An MCP server lets external assistants read and change data. Admins can turn Chat off but cannot block MCP organisation-wide.
Integrations
Packaged connectors are few: SharePoint and OneDrive file links, Microsoft Project XML, Primavera P6 and CSV import, and an MCP server for Claude, ChatGPT, Copilot and Cursor; a full REST API with an OpenAPI document and webhooks is on the standard plan.
Market signal
Teamhood’s homepage (read November 2026) claims more than 1,000 companies in 40+ countries, a largest customer of about 3,000 users and 67 G2 reviews.
Caveat
Teamhood’s four-plan line-up (Personal, Team, Business, Enterprise) was renamed as recently as 3 December 2025; since then new customers get the rebuilt product on a single paid plan, while the earlier product, now Teamhood Classic, keeps those plans for existing customers. The vendor gives no switch date and no support timeline for Classic.
Confidence
Medium-high

Toodledo Dense, long-running task manager with folders, contexts, goals and custom columns, plus notes, outlines, lists, habits and a per-task timer.
PersonalToodledo 2004 Medium $3.99Free plan 20-50 2.8Mean of the six criteria: 2.8 out of 5

Toodledo - summary, assessment and sources

Capabilities

TimeA per-task timer column records actual time against estimated length and can run several timers, but there are no time reports or timesheets.Time tracking: Partial. A per-task timer column records actual time against estimated length and can run several timers, but there are no time reports or timesheets.
BoardsKanban or Scrum boards: Not native.
GanttGantt or dependency timeline: Not native.
CalCalendar view: Native.
SyncA Live iCal Link sends dated tasks one way to Google, Apple and other calendars (Standard and above), and Google refreshes it about once a day.Two-way calendar sync: Partial. A Live iCal Link sends dated tasks one way to Google, Apple and other calendars (Standard and above), and Google refreshes it about once a day.

Summary

Toodledo is one of the oldest web task managers, built for people who want to slice a long task list by folder, context, goal, priority and length. It suits GTD-style planners who are comfortable with a spreadsheet-like screen.

Tasks carry a long list of fields and can be sorted, filtered and saved as searches, with a Hotlist for what matters now. Beside tasks sit notes, hierarchical outlines, custom lists, habit tracking, a scheduler, an in-app calendar and a per-task timer. There is no board, timeline or rule automation, and collaboration is limited to sharing folders with named collaborators.

The free plan stops at 10 folders, 30 items per list and a week of history, and leaves out subtasks and calendar sync. Standard at $3.99 a month billed annually removes most limits; Plus at $5.99 adds the scheduler, file uploads and up to 5 collaborators. Business is sold by quote.

Data sits on US servers at Rackspace with nightly off-site backups; the vendor says only some data is encrypted at rest and publishes no certifications or AI features. Leaving is easy: a backup tool, several export formats and a free API cover the data.

Assessment

Value for money4.3
A free plan for light use, then $3.99 a month for Standard, though subtasks and calendar sync start there.
Ease of use3.2
Many columns, contexts and settings suit dedicated list-makers but take newcomers a while to set up.
Enterprise features1.3
Per-collaborator folder permissions and a quote-only Business plan, but no SSO, audit log or certifications are documented.
Interface flexibility3.0
Custom columns, outlines, lists, notes, habits, goals and a calendar, but no board, timeline or automation rules.
Data control1.3
US servers at Rackspace, only some data encrypted at rest, no certifications, and a 2018 privacy policy.
Portability3.5
Backup and restore, exports and imports in CSV, XML, JSON and iCal, and a free API covering tasks and notes.

Record

First launched
2004. The service dates from 2004, per the vendor’s copyright line, which starts in 2004, and its press page’s “over the last 22 years”.
Vendor
Toodledo, Inc. Privately held; its terms give a New York, USA mailing address and California governing law, and no owners or executives are named.
Website
toodledo.com
Plans
Free; Standard at $3.99 a month billed annually or $4.99 monthly; Plus at $5.99 billed annually or $7.99 monthly with 5 collaborators and 10 GB of files; Business by quote.
Free plan
Free has unlimited tasks with notes, repeats, search and sync, but caps folders at 10, lists and outlines at 30 items, habits at 5 and history at one week, and leaves out subtasks and calendar sync.
Hosting
Servers in the United States, with Rackspace named as hosting provider; redundant storage and nightly off-site backups. No region choice or self-managed edition.
Security
SSL on all connections and two-step authentication; the vendor says some data is encrypted at rest and it is working towards all of it. No certifications, SSO, SCIM or audit log are published. The privacy policy, last updated October 2018, still cites Privacy Shield for EU transfers.
Calendar sync
One-way Live iCal Link to Google Calendar, Apple Calendar and others on Standard and above, placing tasks by start, due and length; Google refreshes it about once a day. A one-off ICS download is also offered.
Data out
Backup/Restore tool plus exports including iCal; imports from CSV, JSON, XML, text and iCal, with guides for Outlook and Remember The Milk. The free API v3 covers tasks, notes, outlines, lists, folders, contexts, goals and locations.
Platforms
Web, iOS and Android apps, desktop apps, and dozens of third-party clients listed in the vendor’s directory.
AI
None.
Integrations
The vendor claims more than 50 third-party apps and tools, mostly sync clients for iOS, Android and desktop, plus IFTTT, a Google Calendar widget and email-to-task on Plus; a free API v3 covers tasks, notes, outlines and lists, with no webhooks documented.
Market signal
The press page claims over a million users and more than 100 million tasks managed (undated, checked November 2026); no revenue, staff or recent growth figures are published.
Caveat
The privacy policy has not been updated since October 2018 and still refers to the EU-US Privacy Shield, which the EU Court of Justice struck down in 2020.
Confidence
Medium-high

Tweek A minimal weekly planner that lays out to-dos like a paper diary, one column per day, with shared calendars and optional calendar sync.
PersonalTweek 2020 Medium $4.17Free plan 8-12 3.1Mean of the six criteria: 3.1 out of 5

Tweek - summary, assessment and sources

Capabilities

TimeTime tracking: Not native.
BoardsKanban or Scrum boards: Not native.
GanttGantt or dependency timeline: Not native.
CalCalendar view: Native.
SyncGoogle event titles, notes, dates and times sync both ways, but Tweek tasks are never sent to a calendar; Outlook imports events, and since October 2026 time changes go back. Premium only.Two-way calendar sync: Partial. Google event titles, notes, dates and times sync both ways, but Tweek tasks are never sent to a calendar; Outlook imports events, and since October 2026 time changes go back. Premium only.

Summary

Tweek is a weekly planner that looks like a paper diary: seven columns, one per day, with tasks written straight into them. It suits individuals, couples and families who want a shared week rather than a project tool.

Unfinished tasks roll over to the next day, ‘Someday’ columns hold undated items, and colour carries most of the organisation. Calendars can be shared with anyone or published as a web page. Month and day views, recurring tasks, reminders and subtasks are there; boards, projects, custom fields and time tracking are not.

The free plan is generous for one calendar. Premium costs $49.99 a year or $5.99 a month and adds calendar sync, reminders, recurring tasks, subtasks, attachments and export, while Family at $89.99 a year covers five people.

The vendor is Scada SIA in Riga, and data lives in Google Cloud Firestore with encryption at rest; the processor list places Google Cloud and DigitalOcean in the USA, and no certification is stated. An AI assistant described in the terms uses Anthropic’s Claude, with OpenAI for voice, and the terms say neither the providers nor Tweek train on your tasks. Export to CSV, XML, TXT or ICS and an open REST API make leaving easy.

Assessment

Value for money4.6
A usable free plan with sharing, then $49.99 a year for one person or $89.99 for a family of five.
Ease of use4.8
A week laid out like a paper diary: type into a day, drag to another; there is almost nothing to learn.
Enterprise features1.0
No admin console, SSO, audit log or certifications; team use means sharing a calendar link.
Interface flexibility2.4
Week, month and day views, Someday lists, colour rules and an API, but no boards, custom fields or projects.
Data control2.0
A Latvian GDPR controller whose Google Cloud and DigitalOcean processors are listed in the USA, with no certifications.
Portability3.5
Per-calendar export to CSV, XML, TXT or ICS on the web, and a REST API even on the free plan.

Record

First launched
2020. Product Hunt launch in 2020 (ranked second of the day on 2 September 2020); Tweek 2.0 followed in June 2022.
Vendor
Scada SIA, Riga, Latvia (EU). Privately held; the App Store lists the copyright as Scada Inc.
Website
tweek.so
Plans
Free; Individual $5.99 a month or $49.99 a year (14-day trial on annual only); Family for up to five people at $9.99 a month or $89.99 a year.
Free plan
Free for ever with one active calendar, two custom colours, notes on tasks and sharing; calendar sync, subtasks, attachments, reminders, recurring tasks and export need Premium.
Hosting
Google Cloud Firestore, replicated across at least three zones in a regional database. The privacy policy lists Google Cloud (cloud services) and DigitalOcean (hosting) as US sub-processors; the Firestore region itself is not named. No region choice and no self-managed edition.
Security
Encryption at rest with Google-managed keys and TLS in transit, per the vendor’s security page. GDPR controller in Latvia. No SOC 2 or ISO 27001 claimed. No SSO, SCIM or audit log.
Calendar sync
Premium: Google Calendar events sync both ways for title, description, date and time (deletions and completion one way, from Google); Tweek tasks are not sent to Google. Outlook Calendar imports events; the help centre still calls it one-way, but the October 2026 changelog says time changes to synced events now reach Outlook. .ics feeds import one way; Apple Calendar and Reminders in the Apple apps; Google Tasks two-way since October 2026.
Data out
Web-only export per calendar and date range to XML, TXT, CSV or ICS (Premium). REST API and MCP server for reading and writing tasks and calendars on every plan, with monthly request quotas.
Platforms
Web, iOS and iPadOS, Android, and a native Mac app (November 2026).
AI
An in-app assistant that answers questions and creates, changes or deletes tasks by text or voice, run on Anthropic’s Claude with OpenAI transcription and Google Cloud (EU) speech. The terms give every plan, free included, its own request limit; the assistant is not yet listed on the pricing, features or changelog pages (November 2026). ChatGPT and Claude apps and the MCP server work on both plans. The terms state neither Tweek nor its providers train AI models on your tasks, messages or voice.
Integrations
Google Calendar, Outlook Calendar, Google Tasks, Linear, .ics subscriptions, and Apple Calendar and Reminders in the Apple apps, plus official ChatGPT and Claude apps. A public REST API and an MCP server work on every plan (15k reads and 3k writes a month free, 150k/30k on Premium).
Market signal
The vendor cites 6,500+ App Store ratings at 4.8 and 3,600+ Google Play ratings at 4.4 (November 2026) and 1,200 Product Hunt followers; no user or revenue figures are published.
Caveat
Tweek tasks never reach Google or Outlook calendars; only synced events can be edited from Tweek (Google fully, Outlook times since October 2026), so it does not work as a time-blocking tool.
Confidence
Medium-high

Workflowy An infinitely nested bullet outline used for notes and to-dos, with any branch viewable as a board, table or dated calendar entry.
PersonalWorkflowy 2010 Medium $6.99Free plan 5-10 3.3Mean of the six criteria: 3.3 out of 5

Workflowy - summary, assessment and sources

Capabilities

TimeTime tracking: Not native.
BoardsKanban or Scrum boards: Native.
GanttTimeline (May 2026) shows the next 30 days and 12 months for drag-to-date scheduling, without dependencies or bars.Gantt or dependency timeline: Partial. Timeline (May 2026) shows the next 30 days and 12 months for drag-to-date scheduling, without dependencies or bars.
CalCalendar is a daily note per date with dated items gathered in, not a month grid of tasks.Calendar view: Partial. Calendar is a daily note per date with dated items gathered in, not a month grid of tasks.
SyncOne-way: Google Calendar events are imported hourly, read-only, for the next 35 days; nothing is written back.Two-way calendar sync: Partial. One-way: Google Calendar events are imported hourly, read-only, for the next 35 days; nothing is written back.

Summary

Workflowy is a browser outliner in which everything, from a shopping list to a book draft, is a bullet that can hold more bullets. It suits individuals who think in nested lists and want notes and to-dos in one place.

You zoom into any bullet to make it the page, tag and mirror items across the outline, and turn any branch into a board, table, to-do list or document. A daily calendar note collects dated items, and since 2026 a timeline and read-only Google Calendar import sit beside it. There is no time tracking, dependency chart or assignee field; @mentions do that job.

The free plan has every feature but caps new content at 100 nodes a month, a limit a daily planner will meet quickly since each bullet counts. Pro costs $6.99 a month on an annual plan or $8.99 monthly, and Teams costs the same per user.

Data is stored on AWS in Northern Virginia, and the privacy policy (February 2026) names no certifications for Workflowy itself. AI chat, AI nodes and actions on Pro send content to OpenAI and Anthropic, which the AI terms say may not train on it. Exports to OPML and Markdown, Dropbox backup and a public API make leaving straightforward.

Assessment

Value for money4.3
Every feature is free up to 100 new nodes a month, then $6.99 a person annually, with free Pro for academics.
Ease of use4.5
One outline of bullets that you indent and zoom into; a new user is productive in minutes.
Enterprise features1.5
Team billing, node-level sharing permissions and MFA, but no SSO, admin console, audit log or certifications.
Interface flexibility3.4
Boards, tables, calendar, timeline, mirrors, templates, AI nodes and an API, all built on one outline without custom fields.
Data control1.8
Data on AWS in Northern Virginia with no region choice and no certifications of its own, under a GDPR-aware policy.
Portability4.2
Whole-account export to OPML, Markdown or plain text, Dropbox backups and a public API with export-all.

Record

First launched
2010. Public release of the web outliner in August 2010, created by Mike Turitzin and Jesse Patel after a Y Combinator startup camp.
Vendor
FunRoutine, Inc., a privately held US company with its official address in Centennial, Colorado.
Website
workflowy.com
Plans
Basic free; Pro $6.99 a month billed annually or $8.99 monthly; Teams $6.99 per user a month billed annually with Dropbox backup and setup help. Free Pro for university staff and students, 50% off for non-profits.
Free plan
Free for ever with every feature, but capped at 100 new nodes a month and 100MB of uploads; past the cap you can still add nodes but are prompted to subscribe.
Hosting
Amazon Web Services in US Northern Virginia, per the privacy policy (updated February 2026); Google Workspace for business operations. No region choice and no self-managed edition.
Security
Emailed one-time codes or passwords, plus optional multi-factor authentication. The policy cites AWS’s ISO 27001/27017/27018 certifications but claims none for Workflowy. No SSO, SCIM or audit log.
Calendar sync
One-way, read-only import of Google Calendar events into the Workflowy Calendar, refreshed hourly for the next 35 days, on all plans. No Outlook or iCloud, and no feed out.
Data out
Any bullet or the whole account exports as plain text, formatted text, Markdown or OPML; tables export to HTML, Markdown or TSV; Pro and Teams add automatic Dropbox backup. Public REST API with an export-all endpoint and a desktop MCP server.
Platforms
Web, macOS, Windows and Linux desktop apps, iOS and iPadOS, Android, and a browser web clipper.
AI
Chat with your notes, AI Nodes and AI Actions for Pro subscribers who enable AI, processed by OpenAI and Anthropic. The AI terms (March 2025) state sub-processors are not authorised to use data for model training.
Integrations
Google Calendar (read-only), Readwise, Kindle highlights, a web clipper, email-to-Workflowy, Dropbox backup and Zapier (inbound recipes), plus a desktop MCP server. A public JSON REST API with API keys covers create, update, move, complete and export-all; no webhooks are documented.
Market signal
No user, revenue or staff figures are published (checked November 2026); the homepage cites ‘over 14 years’ of service and Wikipedia describes a cult following.
Caveat
The free plan’s 100-nodes-a-month cap is a soft limit enforced by prompts, so heavy free use is possible but nagged.

High

Workzone Project management for marketing, creative and operations teams, with Gantt, boards, intake requests, proofing and bundled human training.
TeamsWorkzone 2002 Medium $8†No free plan 5-10 3.1Mean of the six criteria: 3.1 out of 5

Workzone - summary, assessment and sources

Capabilities

TimeTime tracking: Native.
BoardsKanban or Scrum boards: Native.
GanttGantt or dependency timeline: Native.
CalCalendar view: Native.
SyncOne-way webcal subscription of a user’s to-do list (previous 7 and next 30 days) into Outlook or Google; Zapier sync is Enterprise only.Two-way calendar sync: Partial. One-way webcal subscription of a user’s to-do list (previous 7 and next 30 days) into Outlook or Google; Zapier sync is Enterprise only.

Summary

Workzone is an American project management service sold to marketing, creative and operations teams in universities, healthcare, banks and non-profits. Its distinguishing offer is people: onboarding, unlimited training and phone support are included in the price.

Projects are planned as task lists and Gantt charts with dependencies, alongside simpler card boards, a cross-workspace calendar, a personal to-do list and portfolio status reports. Intake request forms, document proofing with markups and approvals, timesheets and workload reports serve agency-style work. Custom fields and critical path arrive only on Enterprise.

There is no free plan and every tier is billed annually. Starter at $8 per user per month suits up to 25 users; Team at $20, with a five-user minimum, is where time tracking, intake and proofing begin. Enterprise is quote-based and charges only for core users, with five free collaborators each.

Data is processed in the United States with no region choice; Workzone states SOC 2 Type II and offers a HIPAA BAA on Enterprise. Its AI runs on an open-weight model inside its own environment and is not trained on customer data. Getting data out is the weak point: the API is a paid Enterprise feature.

Assessment

Value for money2.6
No free plan and annual billing only; $8 Starter stops at 25 users, Team is $20 with five seats minimum.
Ease of use3.0
The vendor plans three to four weeks of human-led onboarding before a team goes live.
Enterprise features3.8
SOC 2 Type II, HIPAA BAA, SAML SSO, enforced MFA and activity logs, with SSO and API held to Enterprise.
Interface flexibility3.8
List, Gantt, Kanban, calendar and portfolio views with intake forms, proofing and dashboards; custom fields only on Enterprise.
Data control3.0
SOC 2 Type II and an in-house AI model, but US-only processing with no region choice.
Portability2.2
Projects export one at a time to Microsoft Project; the API is an Enterprise add-on and no bulk export is documented.

Record

First launched
2002. Service in use since 2002, per a June 2017 vendor press release (“serving diverse industries and projects since 2002”); the about page says only that the company was founded in the early 2000s.
Vendor
WorkZone, LLC, Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, USA (the privacy policy also gives a Blue Bell, Pennsylvania address). Privately owned per a 2017 vendor press release; founded by Rick and Allan in the early 2000s, with no parent company or investors named.
Website
workzone.com
Plans
Starter $8 per user per month billed annually (1 to 25 users, 100 active projects, 3 workspaces); Team $20 (5 users or more) adds time and expense tracking, intake forms, proofing and workload planning; Enterprise is quote-only, charges only core users and adds API, Zapier, SSO, custom fields and HIPAA.
Free plan
No free plan: a 14-day trial without a card, then annual billing on every tier.
Hosting
Primary processing in the United States per the DPA (updated February 2026), with EU Standard Contractual Clauses for EEA transfers; the hosting provider, region and subprocessors are not named, and there is no residency choice or self-managed edition.
Security
SOC 2 Type II; HIPAA support with a BAA on Enterprise; HECVAT and VPAT in the trust centre; encryption in transit and at rest for sensitive stores, hourly off-site backups; activity logs on every plan; SAML SSO on Enterprise; MFA optional or enforced.
Calendar sync
One-way webcal subscription per user, pushing the to-do list (7 days back, 30 ahead) to Outlook, Google or other calendars as all-day events; Outlook events can be imported; Google Calendar and Outlook sync otherwise via Zapier on Enterprise.
Data out
Single projects export to a Microsoft Project file; OData feeds for Power BI and Tableau and an OAuth 2 REST API are Enterprise or paid add-ons. No bulk CSV or JSON export is documented.
Platforms
Web, with a mobile-optimised browser interface for iOS and Android; no native apps.
AI
AI features run on an open-weight model hosted inside Workzone’s own firewalled environment, with no third-party AI providers, no training on customer data and per-user or per-company switches.
Integrations
Native Microsoft Teams, Slack, Google Drive and OneDrive, Outlook import and Microsoft Project export; Zapier, Power BI and Tableau (via OData) and the OAuth REST API are Enterprise or paid add-ons.
Market signal
Workzone publishes no customer or user count; its about page (read November 2026) cites 2.7 million completed projects and a seven-year average customer relationship.
Caveat
Workzone’s API, Zapier connection and SSO are held to Enterprise, and every plan is billed a year at a time, so a team should confirm how it will get its data out before committing.
Confidence
High

Summary

Zenkit Projects is a German work-management service in which every project is a list of items with typed fields that can be shown in eight ways. It suits small and mid-sized teams who want spreadsheet structure and project views in one place, with data kept in Germany.

The same list can appear as a table, Kanban board, plain list, calendar, Gantt chart, mind map, hierarchy or wiki. The Gantt supports dependencies and milestones; critical path, lag and other dependency types need Business. Automations, dashboards and portfolios sit on top. There is no time tracking.

There is no free plan, only a 14-day trial. Plus at $8 per seat (annual) caps the organisation at 10 users and 6 GB; Team at $12 removes the user cap and adds the iCal feed; Business at $21 adds the API, SAML SSO, SCIM and activity auditing. Quotas on items, comments and automation runs apply to every tier.

All data and backups are on AWS in Frankfurt, encrypted at rest, with a GDPR DPA on request; Zenkit cites AWS’s ISO 27001 rather than its own. AI features, priced on request, run in the EU and are not trained on customer data. Lists export to CSV or JSON, so leaving is practical list by list.

Assessment

Value for money2.8
No free plan; $8 Plus stops at 10 users, and API and SSO need Business at $21 a seat.
Ease of use3.6
Lists switch between eight views without setup, but fields, list types and hierarchies take time to learn.
Enterprise features3.4
SAML SSO, SCIM, activity audit and central user management on Business; no certification held by Zenkit itself.
Interface flexibility4.5
Table, Kanban, list, calendar, Gantt, mind map, hierarchy and wiki views with custom fields, automations, dashboards and forms.
Data control2.8
Every account sits on AWS in Frankfurt with an Article 28 DPA, but there is no region choice or own certification.
Portability3.8
Lists export to CSV or JSON with files as ZIP, Trello and Asana importers, but the API needs Business.

Record

2016. Public release of Zenkit in October 2016, per the vendor’s about page; work began at Axonic in 2014.
Vendor
Axonic GmbH, Karlsruhe, Germany (Amtsgericht Mannheim HRB 110424); privately held, managed by Martin Welker. Axonic also makes Zenkit To Do, Hypernotes, Zenforms and Zenchat.
Website
zenkit.com
Plans
Plus $8 per seat per month billed annually ($9 monthly), up to 10 users; Team $12 ($14); Business $21 ($25) with API, SSO, SCIM and activity audit; Enterprise quote-only. Prices cover Zenkit Projects only; Zenkit AI and Zenkit Flow are on request.
Free plan
No free plan on the current pricing page: a 14-day trial, after which an unpaid organisation is usually limited to data export and later deleted.
Hosting
AWS Frankfurt (RDS and S3, contracted through AWS Luxembourg), with encrypted daily backups in a separate Frankfurt data centre. No region choice and no on-premise edition documented.
Security
TLS 1.2+, AES-256 at rest, Argon2 password hashing, app-based 2FA on all plans; SAML SSO, SCIM, activity auditing and central user management on Business; certifications cited are AWS’s (ISO 27001, SSAE 16), not Zenkit’s; GDPR DPA available by email.
Calendar sync
Two-way Google Calendar sync per list, including creating and deleting entries (recurring tasks Zenkit to Google only); Outlook and Apple Calendar only through a one-way iCalendar subscription, which the pricing table places on Team and above.
Data out
Per-list export to CSV or JSON, files as a ZIP, and printing; importers for Trello, Asana, CSV, Excel, Google Sheets and Microsoft Access; REST API on Business and above. After a lapsed trial the organisation is usually limited to export before deletion.

Web, iOS, Android, and desktop apps for Windows, macOS and Linux.
AI
Zenkit AI is sold on request; the vendor says AI runs in the EU, calls models statelessly, does not store inputs or train on customer data, and asks for approval before modifying actions.
Integrations
Built-in Google Calendar sync, Trello, Asana, Excel and Access importers and file-storage connectors; most other links (Slack, Teams, Toggl, Clockify) run through Zapier or Integrately. A REST API is on Business and above.
Market signal
The vendor publishes no current Zenkit user count (about page, read November 2026, cites only 5 million users for Axonic’s earlier products); the English blog’s last post is dated December 2024, while the German blog posts monthly through October 2026.
Caveat
The product is still sold and maintained: the pricing, terms and security pages were revised in October and November 2026, the German blog posts monthly and a Zenkit Processes workflow module appeared in late 2025. But the English blog has been silent since December 2024, no dated public changelog is readable, and the help centre still documents a Free plan the pricing page no longer offers, so confirm plan terms in the trial.

Amazing Marvin - summary, assessment and sources

Summary

Amazing Marvin is a personal task manager and day planner that a Swiss micro-company has run since 2017. It is sold to individuals who struggle with procrastination or ADHD and want to tune the tool to how their own head works.

Every feature is a ‘strategy’ you switch on or off: Kanban boards, a calendar with time blocking, time tracking, habits, goals, a task jar, reward points and procrastination prompts. The result can be a plain checklist or a dense personal system. There are no Gantt charts and no team workspaces; the only AI feature is a braindump sorter in the mobile apps.

There is one plan, Marvin Pro, at $12 a month or $96 a year, with a 14-day trial and no free tier. Students get half price and the vendor offers pay-what-you-can on request, which is unusual. The mobile apps were rebuilt in September 2026.

The privacy policy, last updated in January 2020, names Google App Engine and IBM Cloudant for storage, with US transfers; there are no certifications. Cloud sync can be turned off so data stays in the browser or desktop app. Backups export everything as JSON, and a documented API with webhooks and full database access makes leaving realistic.

Assessment

Value for money3.0
No free plan, and $8 a month annually or $12 monthly is high for a one-person tool, though everything is included.
Ease of use2.8
Over 100 features and 300 settings switched on one by one; productive quickly only once you choose a workflow.
Enterprise features1.0
A single-user tool by design: no admin console, no SSO, and only light task sharing and comments.
Interface flexibility3.8
Lists, Kanban, calendar, smart lists, custom screens and dozens of toggled strategies, plus API and webhooks; no custom fields.
Data control2.4
No certifications and a 2020 privacy policy naming US clouds, but cloud sync can be switched off to keep data local.
Portability3.8
Full JSON backup of tasks, projects and settings, a read-write API and many importers; no CSV export.

Free plan
No free plan: a 14-day trial without a card, after which data is kept but tasks cannot be added or completed until you subscribe.
Hosting
Account data on Google App Engine and task data on IBM Cloudant, with transfers to the USA per the privacy policy (last updated 19 January 2020). No region choice; cloud sync can be disabled to keep data on the device only.
Security
Account data encrypted in transit and at rest, task data in transit (the help centre makes no at-rest claim for tasks), and optional two-factor authentication. No SOC 2 or ISO 27001 claimed. No SSO, SCIM or audit log.
Calendar sync
Two-way sync with Google, iCloud, Yahoo and CalDAV calendars on the single plan; Outlook and Exchange sync is in beta, and public ICS feeds can be imported read-only.
Data out

AI

Integrations
Calendar sync (Google, iCloud, Yahoo, CalDAV, Outlook in beta), Zapier, email-to-Marvin, a browser extension, Siri and Alexa; importers for Todoist, TickTick, Things, OmniFocus and CSV. A REST API with webhooks and direct database access is documented.
Market signal
The homepage claims ‘5K+ happy users’ and the About page names three staff (both checked November 2026); no revenue or customer figures are published.
Caveat
The privacy policy has not been updated since January 2020, so its hosting and transfer statements may not reflect current practice, and it says nothing about the AI braindump added to the mobile apps in September 2026.

Summary

Adobe Workfront runs projects, incoming requests, proofing and approvals, timesheets and portfolio planning in one tenant. It is bought by large marketing, creative and operations departments, often alongside Adobe’s Creative Cloud and Experience Cloud.

Work is organised as portfolios, programs, projects, tasks and issues, with Gantt charts that show predecessors and the critical path, Kanban and Scrum boards, calendar reports and a resource planner. Workfront Planning adds a separate record-based layer for campaign and strategy planning. Calendar sync is now missing: the legacy Home calendar’s Outlook link was removed in October 2024 and the Outlook add-in stopped working in October 2025.

There is no published price and no free plan. Adobe sells Workflow Select, Prime and Ultimate packages by quote, with Standard, Light and Contributor licences; strategic portfolio planning and environment promotion start at Prime, Data Connect and business rules at Ultimate, and Planning and Fusion are separate purchases.

Workfront falls under Adobe Experience Cloud’s SOC 2 Type II and ISO 27001 scope, with data held in the US or in the EU (Ireland, the Netherlands, Germany) as set in the contract. AI Assistant requires a signed Adobe Gen AI agreement and is turning into CX Enterprise Coworker from September 2026. Leaving means row-capped report exports or the REST API.

Assessment

Value for money1.0
Every package and licence type is quote-only, with no free plan and automation through Fusion metered separately.
Ease of use2.0
Access levels, licence types, custom forms and templates need a trained administrator before a team is productive.
Enterprise features4.8
Adobe Admin Console identity, granular access levels, portfolios, programs, resource planning and Experience Cloud certifications.
Interface flexibility4.5
Gantt with critical path, boards, calendar reports, dashboards, custom forms, Fusion automation and a separate Planning product.
Data control4.0
SOC 2 Type II and ISO 27001 under Experience Cloud, US or EU hosting set at contract, but no self-managed edition.
Portability3.0
Report exports to Excel, CSV and TSV stop at 50,000 to 100,000 rows; the REST API is the realistic route out.

2001. Release of @task, the product AtTask sold before renaming itself Workfront in 2015.
Vendor
Adobe Inc. Public company (NASDAQ: ADBE), headquartered in San Jose, California, US; Adobe bought Workfront of Lehi, Utah for $1.5 billion in December 2020.

business.adobe.com/products/workfront.html

Workflow Select, Workflow Prime and Workflow Ultimate, plus Planning Select, Prime and Ultimate and Workfront Fusion automation, all quote-only; older customers may still hold the legacy Select, Prime and Ultimate packages.
Free plan
No free plan; Adobe offers demos, and a free 60-day Workfront Planning trial ran from 2 March to 1 May 2026 for existing Workflow customers.
Hosting
Adobe-run multi-tenant clusters in cloud providers’ data centres. Adobe’s Experience Cloud hosting-locations page (updated 5 November 2026) shows Workfront core processing and storage sites in Oregon, California, Iowa and Virginia in the US and in Ireland, the Netherlands and Germany in the EU, with the location provisioned at contract signing. No Asia-Pacific site, and no self-managed or on-premise edition.

Covered by Adobe Experience Cloud’s SOC 2 Type II, SOC 3, ISO 27001:2022, ISO 27017 and ISO 27018 certifications and HIPAA-ready status; not FedRAMP. Customer-managed encryption keys are not documented.

Workfront Fusion, Adobe’s own integration platform, lists over 70 connectors (Adobe Experience Manager, Creative Cloud, Salesforce, Jira, Slack, Microsoft Teams among them) and is metered by operations; a full REST API and event subscriptions sit beside it, and an MCP server was added in 2026.

Summary

Asana organises work as tasks inside projects, with the same task able to sit in several projects at once. It is sold to whole organisations that want one shared place for team plans, from marketing calendars to cross-functional launches.

Every project can be shown as a list, board, calendar, timeline or Gantt chart, and portfolios and goals roll projects up for managers. Rules, forms and custom fields handle routine workflow. Since 2025 Asana has added AI Teammates and AI Studio, which run agents and automations against a monthly allowance of requests and credits.

The free Personal plan was cut to two users in November 2025, so a team of three must pay from day one. Starter at $10.99 a seat adds timeline and automations; time tracking, approvals and advanced reporting sit on Advanced at $24.99. Above five users seats are bought in steps of 5, then 10 above 30 users, and AI use beyond the included 5 requests per user per month (up to 50 per account below Enterprise) is charged at $0.50 to $0.60 per request.

Asana holds SOC 2 Type II and ISO 27001, 27017, 27018 and 27701 certificates. Data residency in Europe, Australia or Japan, customer-managed encryption keys and audit logs come with Enterprise+, and Asana states that neither it nor its AI partners train models on customer data. Projects export to CSV or JSON, but the full organisation export is Enterprise+ only, so leaving a smaller plan means working through the API.

SAML and SCIM on Enterprise, audit logs, SIEM and residency on Enterprise+, admin console and ISO 27001 certification.

Data residency in Europe, Australia or Japan and customer-held keys through EKM, both on Enterprise+ only.

Summary

Azure Boards is the work-tracking part of Microsoft’s Azure DevOps, the successor to Team Foundation Server. It suits software teams already on Azure, GitHub or Visual Studio who want backlogs and sprints beside their code and pipelines.

Work items follow Agile, Scrum, CMMI or custom processes and appear in backlogs, Kanban boards, sprint taskboards and saved queries; Delivery Plans show up to 20 team backlogs on a timeline with dependencies, and dashboards and Power BI handle reporting. There is no calendar view, and time is tracked as remaining and completed hours rather than with timesheets.

Basic access is free for 5 users and then $6 a seat a month, billed through Azure. Unlimited Stakeholders are free and can edit work items and move cards on a board, but cannot reorder backlogs, plan sprints or configure boards, so whoever plans the work needs a paid seat. Visual Studio and GitHub Enterprise licences include Basic.

Organisations choose one of eight geographies, from the EU to India, and Azure DevOps Server still ships for on-premise use, with Patch 9 released in October 2026. Microsoft lists ISO 27001, SOC 2 Type II, HIPAA and C5. AI arrives through GitHub Copilot, which can turn a work item into a draft pull request. Leaving is done by query exports or the API.

Assessment

Value for money4.3
Five free Basic users, unlimited free Stakeholders and $6 a seat after that, with repos and pipelines in the same licence.
Ease of use2.8
Process templates, area and iteration paths and query-driven views need a configured project before a team is comfortable.
Enterprise features4.6
Entra ID sign-in and conditional access, granular permissions, audit streaming, multi-organisation billing and ISO, SOC, C5 and IRAP coverage.
Interface flexibility4.2
Backlogs, boards, taskboards, delivery plans, queries, dashboards, Power BI views and custom processes; no calendar or list-style planner.
Data control4.8
Eight data geographies chosen per organisation, and Azure DevOps Server remains on sale for fully self-managed hosting.
Portability3.5
Query results export to CSV and Excel and the REST API is complete, but no one-click export of a whole organisation exists.

Summary

Google Tasks is a bare to-do list that lives inside Gmail, Google Calendar and the Workspace side panel, with mobile apps for Android and iOS. It suits people who already plan their day in Google Calendar and want tasks beside their events, not a separate system.

A task has a title, details, a start date and time with a duration, a deadline, a repeat rule, a star and subtasks, and sits in a list. Dated tasks show on the Calendar grid, an email can become a task, and Workspace users can assign group tasks in Chat spaces and Docs. There are no labels, priorities, shared lists, board or timeline.

There is nothing to buy: a personal Google account gets the whole product. Organisations get it with any Workspace edition, from Business Starter at $7 a user per month on an annual plan, which adds administrator control rather than task features.

For Workspace customers Tasks data is covered by Google’s ISO 27001 and SOC 2 scope and by data region policies on Business Standard and above; Gemini can create tasks from any Workspace side panel since September 2026, and Google says prompts are not used for training without permission. Leaving is simple but thin: Takeout gives JSON for the whole account, there is no CSV, and nothing imports in.

Assessment

Value for money5.0
Free with any Google account and already included in every Workspace plan, with no caps a person is likely to meet.
Ease of use4.8
The simplest tool here: a list, a date and a star, reachable from the Gmail and Calendar side panel.
Enterprise features2.5
Workspace admins can switch Tasks on or off and apply SSO and data regions, but Tasks itself has no roles or reporting.
Interface flexibility1.3
Lists, subtasks, stars, deadlines and a calendar display; no labels, priorities, board, custom fields or automation.
Data control3.8
Workspace lists Tasks under ISO 27001 and SOC 2 and data regions from Business Standard; personal accounts get no region choice.
Portability2.5
Google Takeout gives a JSON export of every list and the REST API is free, but there is no CSV or importer.

Summary

Jira tracks work as issues, now called work items, moving through workflows that an administrator defines, and it remains the default tracker in large software organisations. Atlassian also sells it to marketing, operations and other business teams on the same plans.

Every plan has backlog, board, list, timeline, calendar and summary views, custom fields and workflows, and JQL queries that feed dashboards and reports. The timeline shows dependencies within one project; plans across projects, capacity and scenario modelling are Premium. What it lacks out of the box is calendar sync and a timesheet, both of which arrive through the Marketplace.

The free plan stops at 10 users and 2 GB. Prices rose by about 7% on 13 October 2026: Standard is $9.70 per user a month billed monthly for the first 100 users, about $7.92 billed annually, and Premium $19.60. Rovo AI is included on paid plans with monthly credit allowances (25, 70 and 150 per user); SSO and SCIM need an Atlassian Guard subscription below Enterprise.

Data can be pinned to 11 residency locations from Standard upwards. Since 17 August 2026 Atlassian uses de-identified, aggregated metadata from Free, Standard and Premium sites to improve its apps and AI features, and only Enterprise can switch that off; in-app content is also contributed by default on Free and Standard unless an admin turns it off. Leaving is realistic: CSV, XML and Word exports, a full backup with attachments and complete APIs.

Assessment

Value for money3.5
Ten free users and Standard at about $7.92 a user billed annually, but advanced planning needs Premium and SSO needs Atlassian Guard.
Ease of use2.8
Schemes, workflows, screens and JQL reward an administrator; newcomers face unfamiliar terms before the first sprint.
Enterprise features4.8
SAML SSO and SCIM through Guard, audit logs, sandboxes, 150 sites, Atlassian Analytics and FedRAMP Moderate Government Cloud.
Interface flexibility4.8
Custom workflows and fields on every plan, six views, JQL dashboards, rule automation and 6,000 Marketplace apps.
Data control4.2
Residency across 11 locations from Standard, but Data Center stopped selling to new customers in March 2026.
Portability4.0
CSV export to 10,000 items, a full XML site backup with attachments and complete REST APIs; the backup only restores into Jira.

Summary

Microsoft Planner is the task and project tool inside Microsoft 365, reached from the web, Teams and Outlook. Since August 2025 it also carries what used to be Project for the web, so one app now spans a team’s shared board and a scheduled project.

Basic plans give tasks with buckets, checklists, labels and attachments in grid, board, schedule and charts views, plus My Day and My Tasks. Premium plans add a timeline (Gantt) view with dependencies, sprints and backlogs, goals, custom fields and a people view; Plan 3 adds critical path, baselines, roadmaps and an assignments view. There is no time tracking, and premium plans top out at 3,000 tasks each.

Most organisations already have basic Planner through a Microsoft 365 or Office 365 suite. Planner Plan 1 costs $10 per user per month paid annually and Planner and Project Plan 3 costs $30; Planner’s subscriptions page now lists only those two premium plans, and Project Online retired on 30 September 2026. Copilot and the Planner Agent need a separate Microsoft 365 Copilot licence.

Basic plan data sits in Azure in the tenant’s geography and premium plans in Dataverse, under Microsoft’s certifications and data protection addendum; Planner does not take part in Advanced Data Residency or support customer-managed keys. Leaving means Excel exports, an admin PowerShell JSON export or the Graph API.

Basic Planner inside Microsoft 365 and Office 365 suites; Planner Plan 1 at $10 and Planner and Project Plan 3 at $30 per user per month paid annually. Planner and Project Plan 5 (formerly $55) is still named in Microsoft’s Project for the web service description but no longer on Planner’s subscriptions page, which lists only Plan 1 and Plan 3.
Free plan
No standalone free plan; basic Planner (grid, board, schedule and charts views) is included in Microsoft 365 Business Basic and higher suites, but timeline, goals and sprints need Plan 1.
Hosting
Microsoft Azure. Basic plans are stored by the tenant’s default geography: Europe, Americas or Asia-Pacific macro-regions, with local storage for Australia, Canada, India and Japan (UK tenants map to Europe); Microsoft makes no specific residency commitment for Planner and it does not take part in Advanced Data Residency. Premium plans are stored in Dataverse. No on-premise edition (Project Server is a separate product).
Security
Covered by Microsoft 365’s audit reports on the Service Trust Portal, the Product Terms and the Data Protection Addendum. Sign-in through Microsoft Entra ID with its SSO and provisioning; Purview audit logs on all plans, eDiscovery only for basic group plans, no retention policies, and Purview needs an E5-class licence.
Calendar sync
One-way iCalendar publishing of a plan’s schedule to the Outlook calendar (any iCal client can subscribe); assigned tasks also show in Microsoft To Do. No Google Calendar sync and nothing flows back.
Data out
Export a plan to Excel from the web app; global admins can export a user’s plans as JSON with the Export-PlannerUserContent PowerShell cmdlet. Planner API in Microsoft Graph for basic plans; premium plan data is reachable through Dataverse. Direct .mpp import was removed when Project for the web retired.
Platforms
Web, Planner in Teams (Windows, macOS, Linux via the Teams client), Outlook integration, iOS and Android apps.
AI
Copilot in Planner and the Planner Agent (Project Manager agent) require a Microsoft 365 Copilot licence, with more capability for Plan 1 or Plan 3 holders. Microsoft states prompts, responses and Microsoft Graph data are not used to train foundation models, and EU traffic stays within the EU Data Boundary.
Integrations
Built into Teams, Outlook, To Do, SharePoint and Loop, with Power Automate flows and Power BI reporting on premium plans; the Planner API in Microsoft Graph covers basic plans, premium plans live in Dataverse, and a Planner MCP server is documented.
Market signal
Bundled with Microsoft 365 Business Basic, Standard and Premium, Office 365 E1, E3 and E5 and Microsoft 365 A1 (Microsoft Learn, October 2026); Microsoft publishes no Planner-only user count.
Caveat
Microsoft’s own price pages blocked automated access for this review; the $10 and $30 figures are Microsoft’s list prices as quoted in October 2026, and no formal end-of-sale notice for Plan 5 was found.
Confidence
Medium-high

In new Outlook and Outlook on the web a task can be dragged from the My Day pane onto the Outlook calendar to book time; it is a one-way copy and Google Calendar is not supported.

Summary

Microsoft To Do is a plain personal task list built by the former Wunderlist team and given away with every Microsoft account. It suits people who live in Outlook and want their own tasks, flagged email and assigned Planner tasks in one place.

Tasks sit in lists and groups, with steps, notes, due dates, reminders, recurrence and file attachments; My Day is a daily shortlist that empties each night. There is no board, calendar view, timeline, custom field or automation inside the app. Lists can be shared, but there is no assignment workflow worth the name.

There is nothing to buy. Personal accounts get everything free, and organisations get To Do with any Microsoft 365 plan that includes an Exchange Online mailbox; on-premise Exchange is not supported.

Tasks are stored in the user’s Exchange Online mailbox, so work accounts inherit Microsoft 365 encryption, certifications and tenant data location, and admins can find tasks with Purview eDiscovery. Copilot Premium users can read and edit To Do tasks through the Planner Agent since July 2026. Leaving is awkward: there is no export button, only a whole-mailbox PST from Outlook or the Graph API. Microsoft’s task investment has shifted to Planner, and from December 2026 private tasks created in Planner stop landing in To Do.

Assessment

Value for money5.0
Entirely free with a personal Microsoft account and already paid for in most Microsoft 365 work plans.
Ease of use4.7
My Day, smart lists and steps are learnt in minutes, and flagged Outlook email turns up as tasks without setup.
Enterprise features2.5
Work accounts inherit Entra ID sign-in, licence control and Purview eDiscovery, but To Do itself has no team admin or roles.
Interface flexibility1.5
Lists, My Day and smart lists only: no board, calendar view, custom fields or automation inside the app.
Data control3.8
Tasks live in the Exchange Online mailbox under Microsoft 365 certifications and tenant data location; personal accounts get no region choice.
Portability2.0
No export button; data leaves through an Outlook PST export, admin eDiscovery or the Graph API, and there are no importers.

2017. Public preview released in April 2017 by the former Wunderlist team as Wunderlist’s successor.

Microsoft Corporation. Publicly traded (NASDAQ: MSFT), headquartered in Redmond, Washington, USA; To Do came from the team behind Wunderlist, acquired in 2015.

Free plan
Every feature is free with a personal Microsoft account, with no list or task caps published; work and school use needs a qualifying Microsoft 365 licence with Exchange Online.
Hosting
Stored and synced in Exchange Online, so work and school data follows the Microsoft 365 tenant’s data location; personal accounts use Microsoft’s consumer cloud with no choice. No on-premise edition: on-premise Exchange mailboxes have been unsupported since March 2021.
Security
Encrypted at rest on Exchange servers and in transit. Work accounts inherit Microsoft 365 compliance commitments (ISO 27001, ISO 27018, GDPR, EU Data Boundary), Entra ID sign-in with SSO and MFA, per-user licence control and Purview eDiscovery; To Do has no admin console of its own.
Calendar sync
No calendar view or feed. In new Outlook and Outlook on the web, tasks can be dragged from the My Day pane onto the Outlook calendar as a time block (one-way). No Google Calendar sync.
Data out
No in-app export. Personal users export the whole mailbox to PST from desktop Outlook; admins export tasks as PST via Purview content search. The Microsoft Graph To Do API reads and writes lists, tasks and checklist items. No importers.

Web, iOS, Android, Windows and macOS, plus Outlook (web, new Outlook, mobile) and Teams. No Linux app.
AI
No AI inside the To Do app. Microsoft 365 Copilot Premium users can query and edit To Do tasks through the Planner Agent since July 2026; Microsoft states prompts, responses and Graph data are not used to train foundation models.

Outlook tasks and flagged email, Planner assigned tasks, Teams, Microsoft Launcher, Power Automate and Zapier; the Microsoft Graph To Do API covers lists, tasks, checklist items and linked resources for personal and work accounts.
Market signal
Microsoft publishes no To Do user count; its Graph documentation (updated August 2025) says To Do reaches “millions of users”, and the app ships inside Outlook and Teams for Microsoft 365 work accounts as part of a major public company’s product line.
Caveat
Microsoft is moving task management towards Planner: Windows Latest called To Do effectively in maintenance mode in August 2026, and from December 2026 private tasks created in Planner no longer appear in To Do, though no retirement has been announced.

Summary

monday work management is the core product of monday.com, alongside the separate CRM, dev and service products built on the same platform. It is sold to teams of any type that want to model their own process rather than adopt a fixed project method.

Everything lives on boards: rows are items, columns are typed fields such as status, people, date or formula, and the same board can be shown as a table, Kanban, timeline, Gantt chart, calendar or chart. Automations, dashboards and Workdocs connect boards together. There is no native Scrum layer in this product; sprints are sold separately in monday dev.

The free plan is for 2 seats and 3 boards, so it is a trial in practice. Every paid plan starts at 3 seats and is sold in seat buckets. Basic at $9 a seat lacks timeline, calendar, automations and integrations, so most teams need Standard at $12; time tracking, private boards, dependencies and workload sit on Pro at $19. AI runs on monthly credits (1,000 on Basic, 2,000 on Standard, 3,000 on Pro), with more available to buy.

Data is hosted on AWS in the US, Germany or Australia, with the region set by where the account is opened, and monday.com holds SOC 2 Type II and ISO 27001, 27017, 27018 and 27701 certificates. SSO, SCIM, audit logs and strict EU residency are Enterprise features, and the Guardian add-on adds tenant keys and BYOK. monday.com states customer data is not used to train AI models. Boards export to Excel and the GraphQL API is complete, but Workdocs and dashboards are left out of the account export.

Assessment

Value for money2.5
A 3-seat minimum and seat buckets; timeline needs Standard at $12 and time tracking needs Pro at $19.
Ease of use4.3
Colour-coded boards and templates get a team working on day one; cross-board structures take planning.
Enterprise features4.6
SAML SSO, SCIM, audit log, multi-level permissions, portfolios and resource management, all on Enterprise only.
Interface flexibility4.6
More than 30 column types, many board views, dashboards across up to 50 boards, automations and an apps framework.
Data control4.5
US, EU (Germany) or Australian hosting, strict EU residency and BYOK through the Guardian add-on on Enterprise.
Portability3.6
Boards export to Excel with updates; admins get a zip of all boards and files; a full GraphQL API.

Notion Calendar shows and edits database dates beside Google or iCloud events, but tasks are never written into Google or Outlook calendars and there is no iCal feed.

Summary

Notion combines documents, wikis and databases in one editor, so a project plan, its meeting notes and the task list behind it can live on the same page. It is used both by individuals and by whole companies as their internal knowledge base and planning tool.

Everything is a page made of blocks, and databases are pages whose rows are pages. A task database can be shown as a table, board, timeline with dependencies, calendar, list, gallery or chart, and linked to other databases through relations. Notion supplies templates rather than a fixed task model, so assignment, status and recurrence are whatever a team builds. There is no time tracking.

Free suits a single person; teams of two or more hit the block limit. Plus at $10 removes it. Since 13 May 2025 full Notion AI (the Notion Agent, meeting notes and enterprise search) comes only with Business at $20 and Enterprise, and Custom Agents are billed separately at $10 per 1,000 credits. Business also adds SAML SSO and private teamspaces.

Notion holds SOC 2 and ISO 27001, 27018 and 27701, and offers data residency in the US, EU, Japan or Korea on Enterprise; customer-managed keys (Enterprise Key Management) are still a beta for selected Enterprise customers. It states customer data is not used to train AI models; LLM providers keep data 30 days except on Enterprise, where retention is zero. Workspace export to Markdown, CSV and HTML with uploaded files makes leaving realistic, though relations and views do not survive.

Assessment

Value for money3.6
Free is generous for one person and Plus is $10, but full AI, SSO and Agents need Business at $20.
Ease of use3.8
Writing a page is instant; building a working task system from blank databases takes deliberate design.
Enterprise features4.6
SAML SSO on Business; SCIM, audit log, DLP and SIEM connections, residency and beta key management on Enterprise.
Interface flexibility4.6
Table, board, timeline, calendar, list, gallery, chart and form views, relations, database automations and an API.
Data control4.4
Residency in the US, EU, Japan or Korea on Enterprise; customer-managed keys exist only as a beta for selected Enterprise customers.
Portability4.3
Any plan exports the whole workspace to Markdown, CSV or HTML with files; importers cover Asana, Trello and Confluence.

One-way in each direction: a sheet publishes to Google Calendar or any iCal client (Outlook for Windows, not Mac), and a Google calendar can be overlaid read-only on a sheet; edits do not flow back.

Summary

Smartsheet looks like a spreadsheet but behaves like a project tool: each row is a task with owners, dates, dependencies and attachments. It is bought mostly by large organisations and their PMOs, and by operations teams that already think in rows and columns.

A sheet can be shown as a grid, Gantt chart, board, calendar or table, and reports and dashboards roll many sheets together. Formulas, cross-sheet references, forms, approval workflows and no-code WorkApps let teams build their own systems. Much of the advanced range is sold separately: Resource Management (which holds time tracking), Dynamic View from $125 a month, Data Shuttle from $100 a month, DataMesh, Calendar App and Brandfolder.

There is no free plan. Pro at $9 suits a small team of up to 10 Members but lacks the API, timeline view and scheduled backups. Business at $19 needs 3 Members and adds those, plus unlimited automations and workload tracking. SAML SSO, portfolios and directory integration require Enterprise.

Data can sit in the US, the EU (Germany) or Australia through Smartsheet Regions, and a separate Smartsheet Gov runs on AWS GovCloud. Smartsheet lists SOC 2, ISO 27001, 27701 and 42001, with a FedRAMP Moderate authorisation for Smartsheet Gov, and says third parties never train foundation models on customer data. Backups on Business and above are Excel workbooks with comments and uploaded attachments, but formulas, reports and dashboards do not travel.

Summary

Trello is the board most people meet first: lists running left to right, cards moving between them. Atlassian sells it to any team that wants shared visual task lists without the weight of a project tool such as Jira.

Cards carry checklists, due dates, labels, attachments and custom fields, and Butler automation moves them by rule. Power-Ups add almost everything else, from Gantt charts to time tracking, which Trello does not build in. Calendar, Timeline, Table, Dashboard and Map views belong to Premium, and the Timeline has no dependencies. Planner pulls Google or Outlook events beside your cards and schedules focus time back into the calendar.

The free plan is generous on cards and Power-Ups but, since May 2024, a free Workspace with more than 10 collaborators (members, guests and pending invites) turns view-only. Standard at $5 removes the board and collaborator caps; most teams wanting more than boards will need Premium at $10.

Content is held in Atlassian’s US AWS regions, with SOC 2 and ISO 27001 coverage. AI features (board generation, checklists, smart scheduling) are on by default on paid plans. Export is JSON per board for everyone, CSV and Workspace exports with attachments for Premium, and the public API is open on all plans.

Summary

Airtable is a no-code database: each base holds linked tables of typed fields, and teams build their own trackers, content calendars and lightweight apps on top. It suits operations, marketing and product teams who outgrow spreadsheets but do not want a fixed project tool.

Any table can be viewed as a grid, Kanban board, calendar, gallery, form, timeline or Gantt chart, and Interfaces turn bases into custom screens for people who should not see the raw data. Automations, scripting and the Omni AI assistant sit across the whole base. It is not a task manager out of the box: assignment, recurrence and time tracking have to be modelled.

Free allows 5 editors and 1,000 records a base, which suits a trial or a small project. Team at $20 a seat raises that to 50,000 records with Gantt and timeline views; Business at $45 adds SSO, the admin panel and two-way sync between bases. AI runs on monthly credits (15,000 per seat on Team), with top-ups from $20 per 10,000.

Airtable holds SOC 2 Type II and ISO 27001 and 27701 certificates. Data residency in the US, Europe or Australia and customer-managed keys are Enterprise Scale features, and its AI terms bar Airtable and its model providers from training on customer data. Export is CSV per view, so a full exit means using the API. Bending Spoons completed its purchase of Airtable on 4 September 2026 and let go a large part of the pre-acquisition team in October; it says nothing changes for customers’ plans or prices.

A free plan for 5 editors and 1,000 records a base, then $20 a seat, and $45 for SSO and admin.
