Summary

Any.do is a to-do list and daily planner that puts tasks next to the events of your existing calendar, with reminders that can arrive on WhatsApp. It is aimed at individuals and households first, with a Teams plan for small groups who want shared boards.

Personal plans offer lists, subtasks, My Day and a calendar view that mirrors Google, Outlook or iCloud events. Family adds shared boards and a grocery list. Teams adds Kanban, table, calendar and Gantt views, custom fields, task chat, rule automations and time tracking, though the help centre documents few details of the last two.

The free plan has no task cap but holds back recurring tasks, WhatsApp reminders, tags and AI. Premium is $4.99 a month billed annually, and Teams is the same per member with no stated minimum, which makes it one of the cheaper shared boards. Importers from Trello, Asana, ClickUp, Monday and Todoist need Family or Teams.

Data protection is thinly documented: the vendor names no hosting provider, region or certification, and states encryption in transit only. An MCP server lets ChatGPT and Claude read and edit tasks on every plan. Leaving is easier from boards, which export to CSV or Excel, than from personal lists, which print to PDF or export archived tasks as CSV.

Summary

Basecamp organises work as projects, each a page of tools: a message board, to-do lists, a Kanban card table, group chat, docs and files, and scheduled check-ins. It is built for small companies, agencies and anyone who invites clients into the work.

Basecamp 5, released in 2026, added subtasks, a global calendar, account-wide Everything pages and Markdown in documents. Planning stays deliberately light: hill charts show progress by feel, and Lineup places whole projects on a 13-week timeline. There are no custom fields, automations, dependencies or dashboards, and time tracking is a manual timesheet.

Pricing is a flat monthly fee for the account rather than per seat. Freelancer at $29 covers five users and three active projects; Pro at $79 and Pro Plus at $99 raise those to 10 and 15 users. Pro Unlimited, $199 a month billed annually, removes the caps and is the only package with annual billing and the Admin Pro Pack. Large teams pay little per head; a seven-person team with ten live projects already needs Pro Plus.

Data sits on 37signals’ own servers in the United States after its 2023 exit from the public cloud, with no residency choice and no SOC 2 or ISO 27001 certificate. There are no built-in AI features, and the privacy policy says content is not used to train models. Leaving means an HTML archive of every project plus files, or the public API.

Summary

Bitrix24 is a business suite in which tasks and projects share a workspace with CRM, chat, video calls, documents, sites and HR tools. It is sold to small and mid-sized organisations that want one vendor for most of their software.

The tasks module offers list, Kanban, planner, calendar and Gantt views with four dependency types, plus subtasks, checklists, templates, recurring tasks and automation rules. Scrum boards, full time tracking and workload reports arrive on Professional. The breadth is also the cost: the task manager is one item in a long menu, and the interface carries every other module with it.

Pricing is a flat monthly fee per organisation. The free plan has no user cap but stops at 5 GB and one admin. Standard at $99 a month (annual) covers 50 users; Professional at $199 covers 100. Since 1 September 2026 each plan has a cheaper Essentials version without REST API, MCP server or unlimited AI, and a Vibe+ version with them; monthly and quarterly customers move to Essentials limits on 30 November 2026, annual ones at their next renewal.

Cloud data sits on AWS in Virginia or Frankfurt, chosen by the account’s regional domain, and an EU DPA is offered. The self-hosted edition (from $3,590, renewed yearly at half price) includes source code. CoPilot AI is on all plans, sends requests to OpenAI in the USA, and the terms let AI providers use content for development. Leaving the cloud means Excel exports or the API on a Vibe+ plan.

Summary

ClickUp tries to replace a team’s task manager, documents, chat and whiteboard with one Workspace, organised as Spaces, Folders, Lists and tasks. It is sold to teams of every size, and its free plan is a common starting point for small companies.

Few rivals match its range: tasks carry custom statuses, fields and dependencies, and any List can be shown as a list, board, calendar, Gantt chart, table, timeline, workload or mind map. Sprints, native time tracking, goals and dashboards are built in. The cost of that range is density; settings overlap and new users often need a guided setup.

Between late October and November 2026 ClickUp replaced its Unlimited plan with Core at $9 a user and lifted Business to $17 a user on yearly billing, adding a $100 Max plan. Free stays usable for small teams but stops at 60 MB of storage and 100 automation actions. Business is where timeline, workload, dashboards and timesheets live. AI is now included as pooled monthly credits per user, with top-ups at $10 per 10,000 credits.

ClickUp holds SOC 2 Type II and ISO 27001, 27017, 27018, 27701 and 42001 certificates, and offers residency in the US, Ireland, Australia or Singapore on Enterprise. It states that AI partners may neither train on nor retain customer data. Admins can export all tasks to CSV, and importers cover most rivals, though Docs cannot be bulk-exported.

Summary

TickTick is a personal planner that puts a task list, a calendar, a habit tracker and a focus timer in one app. It is aimed at individuals who want to schedule their day as well as list what to do.

Tasks live in lists and folders with tags, sub-tasks, checklists and natural-language dates. The same tasks can be shown as a list, a Kanban board, a Premium timeline with durations, a calendar or an Eisenhower matrix, and a Pomodoro timer logs focus time against them. There are no custom fields, dependencies or automation rules, and sharing is limited to small groups on a list.

The free plan stops at 9 lists of 99 tasks, 2 members per shared list and a basic calendar. There is no team tier.

Data is held on AWS in the United States with encryption at rest and no region choice or certifications. The privacy policy says third-party AI providers process inputs but data is not used to train models. A CSV backup and an Open API make leaving possible, but attachments do not come with it.

Summary

Wrike is a project management system aimed at organisations that run many concurrent projects, such as marketing departments, agencies and PMOs. Its buyers are usually operations leads standardising how dozens of teams plan, approve and report work.

Work sits in an unlimited folder and project hierarchy, with custom item types, workflows and statuses. Projects can be shown as boards, tables, Gantt charts and calendars, and the higher tiers add workload charts, resource bookings, job roles, budgets, file proofing and approval flows. Setup is the cost: Wrike itself recommends a guided deployment for teams of 20 or more.

The free plan, capped at 200 active tasks, suits a small group trying the board and table views. Team at $10 adds Gantt, calendars and dashboards but is capped at 15 users. Business at $25 brings time tracking, request forms and approvals, needs at least 5 users and annual billing, and seats are sold in groups of five. In January 2026 Wrike retired its Enterprise plan for new buyers in favour of Apex, and from April 2026 AI agents run on monthly action quotas.

Accounts are hosted in Santa Clara, California, or Paris, chosen by where the account is registered. Wrike holds SOC 2 Type II and ISO 27001 and 27018, puts SAML SSO and audit reports on Pinnacle, and sells Wrike Lock for customer-managed keys. Its AI addendum says customer data is not used to train models. On Business and above a full account backup exports comments and attachments, but it cannot be restored into Wrike.

Summary

Zoho Projects is a project planner for teams that want Gantt scheduling, timesheets and issue tracking at a low per-seat price. It suits small and mid-sized organisations, especially those already using Zoho CRM, Books or Desk.

Work is organised into projects, phases, task lists and tasks, viewed as a classic list, Kanban board, Gantt chart or calendar, with a separate issue tracker for bugs. Blueprints model approval workflows, and Enterprise adds custom profiles, cross-project dependencies, critical path and baselines. Agile sprints live in a separate product, Zoho Sprints.

Pricing is among the lowest here: Premium is $4 a user per month billed annually and Enterprise $9, with no stated seat minimum. The free plan stops at five users and three projects, and time tracking starts on Premium. SSO, webhooks and portfolio dashboards wait for Enterprise.

Zoho runs its own data centres and assigns a region at sign-up, with migration between regions on request. Zia AI runs on Zoho’s in-house model, and Zoho says customer data is not used for training. The portal owner can export a CSV backup once a day, but the help centre does not say whether attachments are included.

Region chosen at sign-up from Zoho’s own data centres (US, EU, India, Australia, Japan, Canada and others), with ISO 27001/27701.

Owner-run CSV portal backup, XLSX/CSV module exports, a REST API and importers for MPP, CSV, JSON, Jira and Basecamp.

Summary

Superhuman Docs, called Coda until July 2026, is a document in which pages contain linked tables that behave like a database, so a doc can become a task tracker, roadmap or small app. It suits product and operations teams that want to build their own workflow rather than adopt a fixed one.

Any table can be viewed as a grid, Kanban cards, a calendar or a Gantt-style timeline, with formulas, buttons, automations and forms on top. Packs pull Jira, Salesforce or Slack data into tables and push changes back. There is no built-in time tracking, and dependencies that shift dates automatically arrive only on Business.

Billing counts only Doc Makers: Pro is $12 a month billed annually and Business $33, while editors are free. The free plan is generous for small docs but caps shared doc size, attachments and automations. Since the rename, paid plans bundle other Superhuman products, Grammarly on Pro and Mail on Business.

Data is hosted on AWS in the United States with ISO 27001 and SOC 2 Type II; SAML, SCIM and audit logs are Enterprise-only. Third-party AI providers may not train on content, but only Enterprise customers’ AI inputs are excluded from improving Coda’s own AI. Leaving means CSV per table or the API.

Assessment

Value for money4.0
Editors and viewers are free and only Doc Makers pay $12, so a team with a few builders pays little.
Ease of use3.2
A blank doc with tables and formulas, so someone has to build the task tracker before the team can use it.
Enterprise features3.9
SAML SSO, SCIM, audit logs and a SOC 2 Type II report, but all only on the quote-based Enterprise plan.
Interface flexibility4.8
Linked tables with any view, formulas, buttons, automations, cross-doc sync, Packs and AI views make almost any workflow buildable.
Data control3.2
ISO 27001/27017/27018, SOC 2 Type II and HIPAA, but data is stored only in the United States; BYOK is listed as coming.
Portability3.2
Tables export to CSV and a full REST API is open on all plans, but bulk admin export needs Enterprise.

Summary

GanttPRO is a web-based Gantt chart planner made in Poland, aimed at project managers who want critical path and baselines without Microsoft Project’s weight. Its pages now address construction, manufacturing and consulting teams as well as general project work.

Each project is a task hierarchy on a Gantt chart with dependencies, lags and leads, auto-scheduling, baselines and critical path on every plan. Board, list and dashboard views come with Core; calendar view, custom fields and saved filters start on Advanced; workload, portfolios, budgets and time tracking on Business. There is no rule-based automation, and AI is limited to generating a plan from a prompt, voice note or file.

Core costs $8 per user per month billed annually ($7 from 20 seats), Advanced $12 and Business $19, with monthly billing at $9, $15 and $24 and not offered for a single seat. Enterprise, with SAML SSO, custom roles and unlimited storage, is offered at $25 against a $35 list price, annual only and five seats minimum.

Data is hosted on Microsoft Azure in the EU, under ISO/IEC 27001:2022 and a GDPR DPA; OpenAI is the listed sub-processor for AI plan generation. Exports cover PDF, PNG, XML and Excel, and the API and webhooks give a route out, though comments and attachments have no documented bulk export.

Summary

Hive is a work management tool in which every project can be viewed as a Gantt chart, Kanban board, table, calendar or timeline, with chat, email and meeting notes in the same window. It targets mid-sized teams, especially marketing and agency teams that also want proofing and resourcing.

Projects hold action cards with subactions, custom fields and dependencies; portfolio and summary views roll several projects together. Buzz, the AI assistant, drafts content, summarises work and builds workflows. Much of the depth sits in optional apps: proofing, timesheets, resourcing, dashboards, a CRM and a finance module.

The free plan is usable for small teams, but Gantt, calendar and table views stop after 100 uses each. Starter at $5 caps a workspace at 10 members and 10 projects, so most teams need Teams at $12 billed annually. Each add-on then costs about $5 a user per month, so a team with timesheets, resourcing and SSO pays about $27 a seat.

Hive is SOC 2 certified; its privacy policy places data in the United States, and there is no residency choice. AI requests go to third-party models, and Hive says workspace data is not used to train them. Exports are per view in CSV or Excel; there is no single full-workspace archive.

A ten-member free plan and a $5 Starter tier, but timesheets, resourcing and SSO each add $5 a user to Teams.
Ease of use3.6
Projects switch freely between familiar layouts, though the many apps, add-ons and AI toggles take an administrator to arrange.
Enterprise features3.4
SAML SSO and Okta SCIM sit in a $5 security add-on, alongside SOC 2 and portfolio views, with no customer-facing audit log.
Interface flexibility4.4
Gantt, Kanban, table, calendar, timeline, matrix and portfolio layouts, custom fields, forms, workflows and dashboards.
Data control2.6

Cycle schedules subscribe as an iCal feed; issue due dates do not sync, and the Google Calendar integration only reads out-of-office events into Linear status.

Summary

Linear tracks issues for product and engineering teams, grouped into teams, short cycles, projects and company-level initiatives. Its reputation rests on speed and restraint, and it is sold to software companies from start-ups to OpenAI-scale customers.

Issues appear in list and board layouts; projects sit on a timeline with milestones and dependencies, and cycles give each team a sprint rhythm. Triage, customer requests and Linear Asks (Slack and email intake) feed work in. What it leaves out is deliberate: no time tracking, no calendar view and no general custom fields. Since 2025 it has added agents, an MCP server and a cloud coding agent.

The free plan admits unlimited members but caps a workspace at 250 issues, so any real team pays. Basic at $10 a seat (yearly) removes the cap; Business at $16 adds private teams, guests, Insights and Asks. SAML, SCIM and the audit log need Enterprise.

Workspaces are hosted in the EU or the US, chosen at creation and fixed, although account and usage data always stay in the US. Linear holds SOC 2 Type II and ISO 27001 and offers a HIPAA BAA on Enterprise. Its June 2026 terms state it does not train models on customer data. Leaving means CSV exports without comments, or the API.

Value for money3.0
Free seats are unlimited but stop at 250 issues; Basic costs $10 and Insights and private teams need $16 Business.
Ease of use4.5
Opinionated defaults, keyboard commands and fixed issue properties make it usable within an hour, with little to configure.
Enterprise features3.6
SAML, SCIM, audit log, IP restrictions and HIPAA all sit on quote-only Enterprise; Business gets Google SSO only.
Interface flexibility3.0
List, board and project timeline, but no calendar, no general custom fields and dashboards only on Enterprise.
Data control4.0
EU or US hosting chosen at workspace creation on any plan, with SOC 2 Type II and ISO 27001:2022.
Portability3.5
Issue CSVs omit comments and attachments, but the full GraphQL API is open on every plan and four importers exist.

Summary

MeisterTask is a Kanban task manager from MeisterLabs, the Austrian-German company behind MindMeister. It is sold to small and medium teams, especially in Europe, who want a simple shared board with data kept in Germany.

Projects open as a board or a list; tasks carry checklists, tags, attachments, relationships and a built-in timer whose time slips export to CSV or Harvest. Section automations arrive with Pro. Subtasks, custom fields, roles and a Gantt-style timeline arrive with Business. There is no calendar view, and the Windows and Mac desktop apps were withdrawn in April 2025, leaving web, iOS and Android. Redesigned board, list and timeline views are rolling out in beta during Q4 2026.

The free Basic plan stops at three projects and two integrations. Pro costs €12.50 a seat billed annually, but most teams that outgrow a board will be looking at Business at €24. SAML SSO is held back for Enterprise, priced by quote.

Data sits in Frankfurt on Google Cloud under an ISO 27001 certificate, with a GDPR DPA from a German contracting entity. Meister AI uses Google and OpenAI models that, the vendor says, do not train on customer content; only Business admins can switch it off. Leaving means CSV exports per project plus the public API.

Around that sit projects with list, Kanban and Gantt views, custom fields, dashboards, workflow templates, docs and an AI notetaker. Its 2025 ‘AI Employees’ agents had their own pricing grid from August to November 2025; by November 2026 that page redirects to the homepage.

There is no free plan. Teams pay $19 a seat annually for Pro AI or $29 for Business AI, which adds Gantt, time tracking, capacity planning and permissions; a lone user pays more, from $29. Each seat carries a monthly AI credit allowance, with overage billed per 100 credits.

Summary

Podio is a no-code work platform from Denmark, now owned by Progress Software after it bought ShareFile and Podio in October 2024. It suits small and mid-sized organisations that want to build their own trackers, such as CRMs, project registers or request queues, rather than adopt a fixed task model.

Workspaces hold apps that you design from fields: text, dates, categories, contacts, relationships and calculations. Items appear as tables, cards grouped by category, badges, activity streams or calendars, with comments, tasks and visual reports. Simple workflows arrive with Plus and if-this-then-that automation with Premium; there is no Gantt view and no built-in time tracking.

The free plan is only a trial in practice: five users and 100 items across the organisation. Plus at $11.20 per employee adds unlimited items, external clients and read-only users. Premium at $19.20 adds automation (25,000 actions a month), PDF generation and e-signature; extra API and automation capacity are paid add-ons.

Data is hosted on AWS in Dublin under SOC 2 Type II, with security policies Progress describes as conforming to ISO 27001. An AI Assistant is listed as coming soon on Premium, and an MCP server is in beta. Leaving is laborious: Excel exports omit comments and files, so a full copy needs the API or a backup extension.

Each project offers task lists as boards, a table, a Gantt chart with dependencies and baselines, and a calendar, plus timers and timesheets. Proofing and file versioning are its distinctive parts. There are no automation rules, AI features or dashboards beyond reports, and only seven integrations.

Pricing is flat for the whole account with unlimited users. Essential costs $45 a month billed annually but caps the account at 40 projects and 15 GB, and lacks custom roles, workflows, reports and the API. Ultimate Control is advertised at $89 a month billed annually, but that rate lasts three months before rising to $135. There is no free plan, only a 14-day trial.

The privacy policy says data is held in the United States, and ProofHub publishes no SOC 2 or ISO 27001 certification and no SSO. Leaving means CSV exports task list by task list, calendar and timesheet downloads, or the API on Ultimate Control.

Assessment

Value for money3.4
Unlimited users from $45 a month suits big teams, but there is no free plan, and Ultimate Control rises to $135.
Ease of use4.0
Boards, Gantt, chat and proofing sit in one conventional interface that new users and clients follow quickly.
Enterprise features2.0
Custom roles, IP restrictions and activity logs on Ultimate Control, but no SSO, no SCIM and no certifications.
Interface flexibility3.6
Board, Gantt, table and calendar views, custom fields, forms and workflows, but no automation rules or dashboards beyond reports.
Data control1.5
Data is held in the United States with no named certifications, and the privacy policy still cites the defunct Privacy Shield.
Portability2.6
CSV per task list, iCal or CSV calendars and timesheet exports, but no full account export; the API needs the top plan.

Summary

Remember The Milk has been a web to-do list since 2005, run by a small independent team in San Francisco. It suits people who think in tags and saved searches and want reminders to reach them by email or text as well as push.

Everything is a list. Tasks get due dates, priorities, repeats, tags and nested subtasks, mostly typed in one line with Smart Add. Smart Lists are saved searches with almost 50 operators, and MilkScript lets Pro users script changes. There is no board, calendar view, timeline or timer.

The free Basic plan is usable for one person but limits sharing to two others, keeps only a week of completed tasks and leaves out subtasks. Pro costs $49.99 a year and adds Outlook task sync, Zapier, IFTTT, offline web use and the beta AI connector.

Data sits in data centres the vendor does not name, in several locations, and the privacy policy says it is transferred to the United States; there are no certifications. Leaving is straightforward: the account exports to JSON or iCalendar from settings, and a public API with webhooks is open for non-commercial use.

Assessment

Value for money4.5
A free plan with sharing for two people, then Pro at $49.99 a year, about $4 a month.
Ease of use4.0
Smart Add is quick, but getting value from Smart Lists means learning nearly 50 search operators.
Enterprise features1.0
A single-user tool: no team plan, admin console, SSO or audit log.
Interface flexibility2.3
One list view made flexible by tags, saved searches and MilkScript automation on Pro, but no board or calendar.
Data control1.5
Data centres are unnamed and data is transferred to the United States, with no certifications; only encryption in transit is described.
Portability3.5
A self-service JSON export of the whole account plus iCalendar, and a documented API with webhooks, though commercial use needs permission.

Summary

Taskade began as a collaborative outliner and task list and has since rebuilt itself around AI. It suits small teams and solo builders who want shared lists, docs and mind maps alongside AI agents and automations, at a flat workspace price.

Every project is a tree of tasks that can be shown as a list, Kanban board, table, mind map, Gantt chart, calendar, actionsheet or org chart. Tasks take due dates, assignees, custom fields and comments; the timer is a countdown rather than a time log. Since 2025 the product leads with Genesis, which builds small web apps, agents and automations from a prompt.

Free allows two users and no monthly AI credits. Paid plans are flat per workspace: Starter at $6 for three users (annual billing only), Pro at $10 for ten, Business at $25 for unlimited users with SAML SSO. AI credits (10,000 to 400,000 a month) are the real meter, and heavy AI use pushes teams up the tiers.

Data runs in a single AWS US East region. Taskade’s own security page says SOC 2 Type II, ISO 27001 and GDPR compliance are in progress and that it offers no signed DPA. Leaving means per-project Markdown or PDF exports or the REST API.

Summary

Teamwork.com manages client projects alongside the money behind them: time logged against tasks, budgets, retainers, invoices and staff capacity. It is sold to agencies, consultancies and other client-service firms that bill for their hours.

Each project offers list, board, Gantt and table views, with dependencies, milestones, subtasks, custom and formula fields, and a site-wide calendar. Clients can be invited into projects and approve files through Proofs. Resource planning, intake forms and invoicing from logged time arrive on Accelerate; quotes, multi-currency budgets and profitability reports need Optimize.

Pricing was restructured in 2026 into Basics at $9.99 and Accelerate at $24.99 per user per month billed annually, with three- and five-seat minimums. Most agencies wanting capacity planning land on Accelerate, at 2.5 times the entry price. AI features are bundled for an introductory period, with usage-based AI credits due to start in late 2026.

Every plan can host data in the US or the EU on AWS, and the company holds SOC 2 Type II and ISO 27001; SAML SSO costs extra below Enterprise. The vendor says customer data is never used to train third-party models. Leaving is workable: a full MySQL dump, CSV exports and a public API.

Projects, budgets, rates and resourcing sit side by side, so getting value means configuring the client and financial setup first.

SOC 2 Type II and ISO 27001, SAML SSO with auto-provisioning on Enterprise or an add-on, but no documented SCIM.

Summary

YouTrack is JetBrains’ issue tracker, which has grown into a project tool with a knowledge base and helpdesk attached. It is aimed at software teams first, though JetBrains also sells it to legal, marketing and support teams.

Issues carry custom fields and are driven by commands and a search query language. Agile boards run Scrum or Kanban, an interactive Gantt chart (redesigned in 2026.2) handles dependencies, and timesheets and time reports record logged work. Workflows are scripted in JavaScript. A calendar view is the main gap; it arrives through dashboard widgets or Marketplace apps.

The free tier covers 10 users and 3 helpdesk agents with nothing held back. Since 1 October 2025, Cloud costs $4.50 a seat annually or $5.40 monthly, still among the lowest in this category, and every subscription carries the same feature set.

Cloud instances live in one of four AWS regions (US West, Frankfurt, Ireland, Singapore). The self-hosted Server edition remains on sale, and administrators can download a Cloud database backup and restore it into Server. JetBrains states SOC 2 Type II. AI features route to OpenAI and Google, and JetBrains says AI usage data is not used to train models.

Ten free users with every feature, then $4.50 a seat annually, with AI, helpdesk and support included in the price.

Akiflow - summary, assessment and sources

Capabilities

TimeA focus timer exists, but its sessions are excluded from Stats, which report planned durations only.Time tracking: Partial. A focus timer exists, but its sessions are excluded from Stats, which report planned durations only.

Summary

Akiflow is a planner for individuals who juggle tasks arriving from many places. It collects them into one inbox and asks you to time-block them onto your calendar, and it is sold mainly to founders, executives and other heavy schedulers.

Tasks arrive from Gmail, Slack, Notion, Jira, Asana, Linear and about a dozen other tools, then move to Today, Upcoming or a project, and onto the calendar as blocks. An AI assistant, Aki, answers in the app and on WhatsApp, plans days and reads meeting transcripts. There are no boards, Gantt or custom fields, and team features stop at shared availability.

There is one plan, Pro, at $34 a month monthly or $19 a month on an annual plan the vendor has labelled a promotion for a year. The trial lasts seven days and needs a card, and the AI Meeting Assistant costs $19 a month more. That makes it one of the dearest single-user tools here.

Data sits on Google Cloud in a region the vendor does not name, and Akiflow states it holds no SOC 2 or ISO 27001. There is no export button or public API, and in November 2025 support said backup and export were not on the roadmap. An OAuth MCP server is the only official programmatic route, so leaving is hard. AI features are opt-in, and an addendum says content does not train general-purpose models but may be used to debug and improve Akiflow’s own AI.

Assessment

Value for money1.8
No free plan, a card for the trial, and $34 a month monthly or a promotional $19 annually for one person.
Ease of use3.7
Keyboard-first inbox and drag-to-calendar planning are quick to learn, but connecting and triaging many sources takes setup.
Enterprise features1.2
No certifications, no SSO or admin console; team pricing is by quote but adds little beyond availability sharing.
Interface flexibility2.5
Lists, calendar, projects, tags and an AI assistant, but no board, custom fields or automation rules.
Data control1.8
Google Cloud hosting in an unnamed region and no SOC 2 or ISO 27001, though certified under the EU-US Data Privacy Framework.
Portability1.4
No export feature or public API; support points to a SQLite dump from a debug page, and backups are off the roadmap.

Summary

Businessmap, called Kanbanize until 2023, grew from Kanban boards into a portfolio management platform that links OKRs and initiatives to the cards teams move each day. It is sold mainly to mid-sized and large organisations running Lean or Agile at scale.

Work lives on configurable Kanban boards inside workspaces, with initiatives above them on a Gantt-style planning view that supports predecessor links, critical path and milestones. A calendar shows deadlines, cards carry logged time with worklog reports, and flow metrics such as cycle time and blocked time are built in. Business rules automate moves and updates.

There is one feature-complete Standard plan and no free tier. It starts at 15 seats: $10.60 per user annually ($12.70 monthly), falling with volume. Automation rules and SSO cost extra, and Enterprise adds dedicated hosting and support.

Shared accounts are hosted on AWS in the US or the EU, with dedicated instances in other regions for large customers, and Businessmap states ISO 27001:2022 compliance. AI tools draft subtasks, comments and summaries through Azure OpenAI in Sweden or AWS, and the November 2026 privacy policy says this content is not used to train models. Data leaves through Excel exports and the REST API.

No free plan, a 15-seat entry at $10.60 a seat, and automation rules and SSO both billed as add-ons.

Workflows, lanes, initiatives and WIP policies assume Kanban knowledge; most rollouts lean on training or the vendor’s consultants.

Boards, portfolio workspaces, Gantt planning view, calendar, OKRs, whiteboards, dashboards, flow analytics and IF-THEN business rules.
Data control4.2
EU (Dublin, Frankfurt) or US hosting on shared plans, with dedicated AWS instances in other regions on request.

Search results export to Excel and add-ins sync with Excel or Sheets, but there is no full-account JSON export.

Summary

Celoxis is a project portfolio management system that has been sold since 2001, built in Pune for PMOs that run scheduled projects alongside resource capacity, budgets and billing. Its buyers are manufacturing, technology, healthcare and services firms rather than small teams.

Plans are task hierarchies with all four dependency types, constraints, baselines and critical path. Every report can be shown as a table, Gantt, calendar, card board with draggable lanes or chart, and dashboards are built from those reports. Timesheets with timers and approvals, expenses, risks and issues and custom workflow apps sit beside the projects. Scrum is handled by convention, with sprints as summary tasks, rather than as a dedicated mode.

Core costs $10 per full-access user per month billed annually, with a five-user minimum, and already includes workload tracking and capacity planning; timesheets cost $5 more on Core or come with Essentials at $25, which adds job roles and resource-conflict checks. Project billing, the client portal and an undefined “advanced security” bundle need Business at $45. Enterprise, which includes the on-premise licence, is quoted.

The cloud runs on AWS with a choice of US or Ireland data centres, under ISO 27001 and SOC 2 Type II, and a self-hosted edition runs on PostgreSQL, SQL Server or Oracle. The Lex assistant uses Microsoft Azure AI Services and is not priced separately. Exports are CSV and PDF; the REST API and webhooks are the fuller route out.

Summary

Favro is a Swedish planning tool built by the founders of an earlier enterprise agile product. It is sold to teams that run several boards in parallel, especially game studios and software companies, and to managers who need to see across them.

Its distinctive idea is that one card can live on several boards at once, so a task appears on a team’s Kanban board, a manager’s sheet and a roadmap without copying. Collections group boards; backlogs nest cards into hierarchies; relations, dependencies, burndowns, dashboards, forms, documents and a calendar sit on top, and rule-based automations move work along.

There is no free plan. Lite at $5.10 a user is limited to five collections, 25 automation actions a month and no integrations or API, so most teams will need Standard at $6.80. Users are billed in buckets from two seats, and timesheets, SAML SSO and SCIM are Enterprise only.

Data stays in the EU on AWS Frankfurt and Cleura in Sweden, under ISO 27001 and 27701 certificates and a DPA. Favro has no built-in AI and charges no AI fees; an official MCP server lets Claude, ChatGPT or Cursor act on your behalf. Leaving means board-by-board exports or the API on Standard.

Summary

Fibery is a configurable workspace in which a team defines its own databases (tasks, features, clients, objectives) and links them, then works on them through views, documents and automations. It suits product teams, agencies and start-ups that want one tool shaped to their process.

Every database can be shown as a board, table, list, timeline with dependencies, Gantt, calendar, gallery, feed or map, with charts and dashboards over the data; whiteboards and collaborative documents link to entities. Rules, buttons and JavaScript scripts automate work. The cost of that freedom is set-up: nothing works until someone designs it, and time tracking is something you build.

The free plan covers 10 users and 10 databases. Standard at $12 a seat (annual) adds unlimited databases, charts and whiteboards; Pro at $20 adds custom apps, advanced permissions, JavaScript automations and shared Gantt views; Enterprise at $40, from 25 seats, brings SAML, SCIM and regional hosting.

Data is hosted on AWS in the EU unless an Enterprise customer chooses the US, UK or APAC, and Fibery holds a SOC 2 Type II report. Its AI terms forbid providers from training on inputs or outputs. Leaving is straightforward: a full Markdown and CSV export on every plan, plus REST and GraphQL APIs.

Assessment

Value for money3.6
Ten free users with real databases, then $12 a seat; SSO needs the $40 Enterprise plan with 25 seats minimum.
Ease of use2.5
A blank workspace means designing databases, relations and views first; Fibery itself calls the people who do this Architects.
Enterprise features3.6
SOC 2 Type II, audit logs and granular sharing, but SAML, SCIM and IP restrictions arrive only on Enterprise.
Interface flexibility4.9
Custom databases and relations, formulas, ten view types, charts, whiteboards, JavaScript automations and AI-built custom apps.
Data control3.8
EU hosting by default with SOC 2 Type II; US, UK or APAC residency only on the Enterprise plan.
Portability4.3
Any plan can export the whole workspace as Markdown and CSV, with REST and GraphQL APIs and CSV import.

Summary

Freedcamp is a long-running, low-cost project workspace from a small Californian company. It suits small businesses, schools and non-profits that want several teams in one place without per-seat bills, and offers discounts to education and non-profit users.

A project bundles separate apps: tasks shown as a list, Kanban board or table, a calendar, milestones, time tracking, discussions, files and a password store. Business adds a Gantt chart with dependencies, critical path and slack time, plus a wiki, issue tracker, CRM, invoices, reports, custom fields and custom statuses. There is no general rules engine for automation; recurring tasks are the main exception.

The free plan has no user or project cap, which is rare. Pro at $1.49 adds table view, subtasks, recurring tasks, Google Calendar push and cloud-file links, but most teams will want Business at $7.49 for the Gantt and custom fields. Guests and read-only collaborators cost nothing.

Data sits on AWS in the US; Freedcamp cites AWS certifications rather than its own and handles EU transfers through the Data Privacy Framework. Leaving relies on per-app XLS exports, which omit comments, or Business backups in XLS and XML with attachments, plus the public API.

Summary

Nifty gathers a project’s milestones, tasks, documents, files and team chat in one workspace, with each project opening on a roadmap of milestones. It is aimed at agencies, product teams and small companies that work with clients.

Projects combine a Gantt-style milestone roadmap with task lists, Kanban and swimlane boards, and team calendars. Tasks carry custom fields, dependencies, story points and timers. Portfolios, workloads, goals and automatic check-ins roll work up across projects, and clients join as guests. Orbit AI drafts documents and generates projects and tasks.

Pricing comes in two forms: per-member plans (Pro $10, Business $16 billed annually) for small teams, and flat bundles (Pro $79 for 10 members, Business $124 for 30, Unlimited $399) for larger ones. Data sits on AWS under SOC 2 and ISO 27001:2022 audits, with no region choice. Orbit AI sends content to OpenAI, which Nifty says may not train on it. Leaving is harder than arriving: importers cover nine tools, but there is no documented workspace export.

Summary

Work is organised as spaces, projects, sections and tasks, with an Incoming list for anything needing a person’s attention and a Priority list for their own day. A calendar view shows dated tasks, and AI can build a project from a description or a CSV file. There is no board, Gantt or custom field, and time tracking is manual fields only.

The free plan covers three people and three projects. Premium is $9 per user per month (annual) for a single space; Business at $15 adds one subscription across spaces and unlimited admins. Per-user prices fall from ten users.

Nozbe AI uses Gemini; the vendor makes no statement on training. Task lists export to CSV, support will send a ZIP archive of all data, and a documented REST API makes leaving straightforward.

Summary

OmniFocus is the Omni Group’s task manager for people who run their lives by David Allen’s Getting Things Done. It is built for Mac, iPhone, iPad, Apple Watch and Vision Pro, and since 2019 the same database can also be reached from any browser.

Actions sit in projects and folders, carry tags, due, planned and defer dates, and can be sequential so only the next step shows. Custom perspectives filter the whole database, and a weekly review keeps it current. There are no boards, calendar grid, Gantt, time tracking or sharing. OmniFocus for the Web is a companion: you must set up the database in an Apple app first, and it lacks the review, notifications and repeat editing.

There is no free plan. The $99.99 annual subscription includes the Pro apps and web access. Owners of a $74.99 or $149.99 perpetual licence pay $49.99 a year more for the browser. For someone without an Apple device the web app is not usable on its own.

Sync uses end-to-end encryption with a passphrase you choose, and the Apple apps can sync through your own WebDAV server instead of Omni’s, though the web app cannot. There are no published certifications. The Apple apps export CSV, HTML and plain text; AI is limited to on-device Apple Intelligence date parsing and Siri in beta.

Assessment

Value for money3.0
No free plan; $99.99 a year covers every Apple device and the web, or $49.99 a year on top of a licence.
Ease of use2.6
Defer dates, sequential projects and perspectives reward GTD practitioners but take weeks to learn; web setup needs an Apple device.
Enterprise features1.0
A single-user tool: no shared projects, admin console, SSO or certifications; business purchasing is just volume licensing.
Interface flexibility2.8
Custom perspectives and Omni Automation scripting go deep, but every view is an outline, and the web lacks review and repeats.
Data control3.6
End-to-end encryption with your own passphrase and optional self-hosted WebDAV sync, though the web app requires Omni’s sync server.
Portability3.0
CSV, HTML and plain-text exports plus automatic backups in the Apple apps; no REST API and no export from the web.

The Apple apps export to CSV, HTML and plain text, keep automatic backups and allow database migration; Omni Automation (Pro) and AppleScript (Mac) script the data on device. No REST API. The web app can view and download attachments but has no export.

macOS, iOS, iPadOS, watchOS and visionOS apps, plus OmniFocus for the Web in a desktop browser (designed for computers rather than phones). No native Windows, Linux or Android apps.
AI
On-device only: optional Apple Intelligence date parsing (beta) and Siri AI reminder integration (beta) in OmniFocus 4.9, September 2026; neither runs in the web app. Omni’s privacy page says customer data is not shared with advertising or social-media services.
Integrations
Apple-platform hooks: Siri (Siri AI beta in 2026), Shortcuts, Share Sheet, Apple Reminders capture, Mail Drop email capture and Omni Automation JavaScript plug-ins (Pro). No REST API, webhooks or Zapier connector; the web app has no integrations.
Market signal
No user or revenue figures are published; the About page lists 28 staff (November 2026), and OmniFocus has been a fixture of Apple-platform GTD since 2008.
Caveat
OmniFocus for the Web is not a standalone product: it needs a database first set up in an Apple app, and it lacks review, notifications and repeat editing.
Confidence
High

Summary

Paymo began in 2007 inside a small web agency as a way to see where billable hours went, and it is still built around that loop: track time on tasks, then invoice the client. It suits freelancers and agencies of up to a few dozen people.

Projects hold task lists with list, table, calendar and Kanban views, plus a meta-Kanban board across projects. Time comes from in-app timers, desktop and mobile apps or the automatic Paymo Track, and feeds timesheets, estimates, invoices, expenses and profitability reports. Pro adds Gantt charts with dependencies, a portfolio Gantt, team scheduling with workload, timesheet approvals and leave planning. There is no AI and no workflow automation.

The free plan is for one person with one client and two projects. Solo costs $5.90 a month billed annually for one user; teams need Plus at $10.90 per user billed annually ($15.90 monthly), which also unlocks integrations and the API, or Pro at $16.90 for scheduling and Gantt.

Data is hosted on Amazon Web Services; Paymo publishes no certifications or region and offers no SAML SSO, though two-factor authentication and Google or Apple sign-in are available. The open REST API, with webhooks, covers all account data including comments and files, which makes a scripted exit realistic, while in-app exports are per report or table.

Summary

Plaky is a board-based work tracker from CAKE.com, the company behind the Clockify time tracker. It is aimed at small and mid-sized teams wanting a cheap, monday.com-style tool, and is free for any number of users.

Each board is a table of items with typed fields, viewable as a table, Kanban board, Gantt chart or pie and bar charts, with dashboards across boards and rule-based automations. The Gantt shows bars and subitems but no documented dependencies, and there is no calendar view or calendar sync. Time tracking works only by connecting a Clockify workspace.

The free plan has no user cap but limits boards to 6 fields and keeps a 7-day activity log. Pro at $3.99 per seat (annual) adds Gantt, unlimited fields, private boards and 1,000 automation actions a month; Enterprise at $8.99 adds SSO, board permissions and an unlimited log. The $12.99 CAKE.com Bundle includes Clockify and Pumble.

CAKE.com states ISO 27001:2022 and SOC 2 Type II at company level without naming the products covered, and says most processing is in the United States, with AWS, Microsoft and Hetzner as subprocessors; no Plaky data-region choice is documented. No AI features are listed. Leaving means per-board CSV exports, which omit comments, or the public API released in January 2026.

Spreadsheet-like boards with status columns that a new team can fill in within minutes.

SSO, board ownership and protected views on Enterprise at $8.99; CAKE.com’s ISO 27001 and SOC 2 name no products in scope; no SCIM.

Table, Kanban, Gantt and chart views with dashboards and automations, but no calendar view and a 6-field free cap.

Quire is built around one idea: a task list that nests without limit, so a project breaks down into subtasks of subtasks and every other view reads from that tree. It is aimed at small teams and planners who think in outlines rather than boards.

The same tasks appear as a nested list, a Kanban board, a timeline with finish-to-start dependencies, a calendar, a table, dashboards and insight charts. Sublists and smart folders slice work across projects, and collaborative documents sit beside the tasks. Data is held on AWS in the United States under an ISO 27001:2022 certificate, and the privacy policy says it is processed in the US and Taiwan. Quire has no built-in AI assistant; instead an MCP server and CLI let outside AI tools read and write tasks. Exports in CSV and JSON plus a public API make leaving practical.

Redbooth is still sold and updated (web forms and public links in October 2026; iOS app 8.81 on 20 October 2026), but its terms and DPA name no legal entity or governing law, and its security page still relies on the Privacy Shield framework invalidated in 2020, with a sentence naming another company, Notion Inc.

Summary

Shortcut, called Clubhouse until 2021, organises software work as stories grouped into epics, timed into iterations and tied to objectives. It is sold to product and engineering teams that want sprints and a roadmap without Jira’s administration.

Stories move across Kanban boards through custom workflows; a backlog, a roadmap with table and timeline layouts, built-in docs and reports for velocity, cycle time and cumulative flow sit alongside. The roadmap timeline draws no dependencies, there is no calendar view and no time tracking. Korey, an AI agent launched in September 2025, drafts specs and stories and hands work to coding agents.

The free plan covers 10 users with one team and one workflow. Team at $8.50 a seat (yearly) adds automations, WIP limits, five workflows and the calendar feed; Business at $12 adds unlimited teams, objectives and key results, advanced custom fields and extra workspaces. SSO costs extra until Enterprise.

Data sits on AWS with SOC 2 Type II audits and backups every 10 minutes; there is no region choice. Korey is priced per organisation, and Shortcut says Korey inputs and outputs are not used for training. Leaving means CSV story exports or the API, with importers in from Jira, Trello, Linear and Pivotal Tracker.

Ten free users with sprints and a roadmap, then $8.50 a seat; custom fields and objectives wait for $12 Business.

Stories, epics and iterations map directly onto how software teams already talk, and the board needs little setup.
Enterprise features2.8
SAML and Okta-only SCIM are add-ons below Enterprise, there is no customer-facing audit log, and SOC 2 reports are by request.
Interface flexibility3.3
Boards, backlog, roadmap table and timeline, docs, burndown and cycle-time reports and custom workflows, but no calendar view.
Data control2.8
SOC 2 Type II and a HIPAA BAA, but one AWS hosting location with no residency choice and no self-managed edition.

Story CSVs leave out comments, but the REST API is open on every plan and importers cover Jira, Trello, Linear and Pivotal.

Summary

Sunsama is a daily planner for knowledge workers who want each morning to start with a deliberate plan. It is sold per person, with a shared-workspace option for teams who want one bill.

The core object is a task placed on a day. A board of day columns sits beside your real calendar, and you drag tasks into time slots that write back to Google, Outlook or iCloud. Integrations pull issues, cards and emails in from Jira, Asana, Linear, Gmail and about 20 other tools. There are channels, weekly objectives and a timer, but no projects in the usual sense, no custom fields and no Gantt.

There is one self-serve plan, Pro, at $17 a month billed annually or $22 monthly, and no free tier. That single plan replaced a short-lived split into Basic Pro and Power Pro in spring 2026, and it still makes Sunsama one of the dearest per-seat tools in this comparison for a single person.

All data is stored in the United States on Google Cloud, MongoDB Atlas and AWS. SOC 2 Type II arrived in late 2025, and SSO, SCIM and audit logs sit on a quote-only Enterprise tier. The AI assistant, Sunny, and the MCP server are on Pro, and the privacy policy says customer data never trains models. Leaving relies on a whole-history export, since there is no public API.

A list is a document: tasks sit beside text, headers and images, and each task opens into its own page of subtasks, notes and attachments. Lists can be shared with assignees and comments. Summary

TeamGantt is a Gantt chart scheduler that started in 2009 as a tool for a Baltimore roofing contractor, and it has gone back to those roots: its pages now speak mostly to home builders, remodelers and trade contractors, though any small team can use it.

A project is a Gantt chart with groups, tasks, milestones and dependencies, with critical path on every plan; list and calendar views come everywhere, while Kanban, workload, time tracking, portfolios and advanced dependencies start at Business. Builder Edition adds lookahead schedules, material lead times and a Procore sync. Custom workflows are reserved for Builder Edition, and other automation runs through Zapier.

Pricing is by account and project rather than seat. Base is $589 a year for 1 manager, 10 collaborators and 5 projects of up to 150 tasks; Business is $1,140 a year with unlimited people and 5 projects, then $24 a month per project up to 20. Trials need a card.

Data is stored in the United States on AWS with nightly backups; TeamGantt publishes no certifications, no DPA and nothing on how its AI project creation handles data. Leaving is easier: each project exports to CSV, PDF or MS Project, and the REST API covers tasks, time, comments and files.

No per-seat bill, but Base caps at five projects and Business charges $24 a month for each project beyond five.

Summary

Teamhood is a project planning service from a Lithuanian company that now sells mainly to engineering, architecture and other technical firms running many projects with the same people. Its pitch is resource planning: showing each person’s planned hours across every project so overbooking is visible.

Work is built from configurable item types and fields, shown in list, board, Gantt, schedule, mind map, timesheet and chart views. The Gantt reschedules dependent items, keeps baselines and previews what a change will move; the schedule view becomes a capacity plan when grouped by person. There is no calendar view, no calendar sync and no mobile app.

The current product has one paid plan at $12 (€11) per user per month billed annually, with a three-licence minimum and guests counted as members. There is no free plan, only a one-month trial. Enterprise is quote-only. Customers of the earlier Teamhood Classic keep its separate four-plan structure.

Data sits on Microsoft Azure in the EU; Enterprise can choose Germany or the US, or run dedicated, hybrid or on-premise installations. Teamhood holds no ISO 27001 or SOC 2 of its own. The Chat assistant uses OpenAI with stored responses off. List views export to Excel and CSV and the REST API reads everything, but only while the subscription is paid.

Assessment

Value for money2.8
No free plan and a three-licence minimum at $12, though API, AI chat and resource planning are all included.
Ease of use3.1
Configurable item types, fields and roles suit planners, but a new team has setup to do before it works.
Enterprise features3.3
Custom roles, portfolio views and forced two-factor sign-in; SSO and SCIM only on quote-based Enterprise, and no own certification.
Interface flexibility4.0
List, board, Gantt, schedule, mind map, timesheet and chart views with formula fields, templates and rollups, but no calendar.
Data control4.5
EU Azure hosting by default, with Enterprise choices of Germany, US, dedicated, hybrid or on-premise installation.
Portability4.0
Excel and CSV export from list views and a full REST API, but a lapsed organisation cannot read its own data.

2020. Approximate: a 2024 vendor blog post says the first Teamhood version went live four years and 100 releases earlier, and a May 2021 press release already describes an upgrade of the platform; Eylean itself dates from 2011.
Vendor
UAB Eylean, Vilnius, Lithuania. Privately held; makers of Eylean Board since 2011, with Vidas Vasiliauskas as CEO.

teamhood.com

Teamhood $12 (€11) per user per month billed annually or $16 (€14) monthly, minimum 3 licences; Enterprise is quote-only and adds SSO, SCIM, invoice billing and dedicated, hybrid or on-premise hosting. Existing customers on Teamhood Classic keep its Personal (free), Team, Business and Enterprise plans.
Free plan
No free plan: the first month is a free trial without a card, after which every member, open invite and guest needs a paid licence.
Hosting
Microsoft Azure in the EU with failover to another EU region; Enterprise can pick the EU, Germany or the US, or dedicated, hybrid (database on the customer’s servers) or on-premise hosting with customer-installed updates.
Security
Teamhood states it holds neither ISO 27001 nor SOC 2 (Azure does); TLS in transit, encryption at rest, hourly backups with 7-day point-in-time restore, organisation-wide 2FA on every plan; SSO and SCIM on Enterprise; a DPA from UAB Eylean lists subprocessors.
Calendar sync
None documented: no Google or Outlook sync and no iCal feed.
Data out
List views export visible columns to Excel or CSV; timesheets export with cost; Gantt downloads as PDF; a REST API (200 requests a minute per organisation) and webhooks read everything, including per-item history. A lapsed organisation is closed and cannot export until renewed.

Web only; the vendor states there are no mobile apps.

In-app Chat on every licence uses OpenAI with stored responses turned off; OpenAI keeps API data up to 30 days for abuse checks and does not train on it. An MCP server lets external assistants read and change data. Admins can turn Chat off but cannot block MCP organisation-wide.
Integrations
Packaged connectors are few: SharePoint and OneDrive file links, Microsoft Project XML, Primavera P6 and CSV import, and an MCP server for Claude, ChatGPT, Copilot and Cursor; a full REST API with an OpenAPI document and webhooks is on the standard plan.
Market signal
Teamhood’s homepage (read November 2026) claims more than 1,000 companies in 40+ countries, a largest customer of about 3,000 users and 67 G2 reviews.

Teamhood’s four-plan line-up (Personal, Team, Business, Enterprise) was renamed as recently as 3 December 2025; since then new customers get the rebuilt product on a single paid plan, while the earlier product, now Teamhood Classic, keeps those plans for existing customers. The vendor gives no switch date and no support timeline for Classic.

Summary

Toodledo is one of the oldest web task managers, built for people who want to slice a long task list by folder, context, goal, priority and length. It suits GTD-style planners who are comfortable with a spreadsheet-like screen.

Tasks carry a long list of fields and can be sorted, filtered and saved as searches, with a Hotlist for what matters now. Beside tasks sit notes, hierarchical outlines, custom lists, habit tracking, a scheduler, an in-app calendar and a per-task timer. There is no board, timeline or rule automation, and collaboration is limited to sharing folders with named collaborators.

The free plan stops at 10 folders, 30 items per list and a week of history, and leaves out subtasks and calendar sync. Standard at $3.99 a month billed annually removes most limits; Plus at $5.99 adds the scheduler, file uploads and up to 5 collaborators. Business is sold by quote.

Data sits on US servers at Rackspace with nightly off-site backups; the vendor says only some data is encrypted at rest and publishes no certifications or AI features. Leaving is easy: a backup tool, several export formats and a free API cover the data.

Assessment

Value for money4.3
A free plan for light use, then $3.99 a month for Standard, though subtasks and calendar sync start there.
Ease of use3.2
Many columns, contexts and settings suit dedicated list-makers but take newcomers a while to set up.
Enterprise features1.3
Per-collaborator folder permissions and a quote-only Business plan, but no SSO, audit log or certifications are documented.
Interface flexibility3.0
Custom columns, outlines, lists, notes, habits, goals and a calendar, but no board, timeline or automation rules.
Data control1.3
US servers at Rackspace, only some data encrypted at rest, no certifications, and a 2018 privacy policy.
Portability3.5
Backup and restore, exports and imports in CSV, XML, JSON and iCal, and a free API covering tasks and notes.

Servers in the United States, with Rackspace named as hosting provider; redundant storage and nightly off-site backups. No region choice or self-managed edition.

SSL on all connections and two-step authentication; the vendor says some data is encrypted at rest and it is working towards all of it. No certifications, SSO, SCIM or audit log are published. The privacy policy, last updated October 2018, still cites Privacy Shield for EU transfers.

Google event titles, notes, dates and times sync both ways, but Tweek tasks are never sent to a calendar; Outlook imports events, and since October 2026 time changes go back. Premium only.

Summary

Tweek is a weekly planner that looks like a paper diary: seven columns, one per day, with tasks written straight into them. It suits individuals, couples and families who want a shared week rather than a project tool.

Unfinished tasks roll over to the next day, ‘Someday’ columns hold undated items, and colour carries most of the organisation. Calendars can be shared with anyone or published as a web page. Month and day views, recurring tasks, reminders and subtasks are there; boards, projects, custom fields and time tracking are not.

The free plan is generous for one calendar. Premium costs $49.99 a year or $5.99 a month and adds calendar sync, reminders, recurring tasks, subtasks, attachments and export, while Family at $89.99 a year covers five people.

The vendor is Scada SIA in Riga, and data lives in Google Cloud Firestore with encryption at rest; the processor list places Google Cloud and DigitalOcean in the USA, and no certification is stated. An AI assistant described in the terms uses Anthropic’s Claude, with OpenAI for voice, and the terms say neither the providers nor Tweek train on your tasks. Export to CSV, XML, TXT or ICS and an open REST API make leaving easy.

Assessment

Value for money4.6
A usable free plan with sharing, then $49.99 a year for one person or $89.99 for a family of five.
Ease of use4.8
A week laid out like a paper diary: type into a day, drag to another; there is almost nothing to learn.
Enterprise features1.0
No admin console, SSO, audit log or certifications; team use means sharing a calendar link.
Interface flexibility2.4
Week, month and day views, Someday lists, colour rules and an API, but no boards, custom fields or projects.
Data control2.0
A Latvian GDPR controller whose Google Cloud and DigitalOcean processors are listed in the USA, with no certifications.
Portability3.5
Per-calendar export to CSV, XML, TXT or ICS on the web, and a REST API even on the free plan.

Summary

Workflowy is a browser outliner in which everything, from a shopping list to a book draft, is a bullet that can hold more bullets. It suits individuals who think in nested lists and want notes and to-dos in one place.

You zoom into any bullet to make it the page, tag and mirror items across the outline, and turn any branch into a board, table, to-do list or document. A daily calendar note collects dated items, and since 2026 a timeline and read-only Google Calendar import sit beside it. There is no time tracking, dependency chart or assignee field; @mentions do that job.

The free plan has every feature but caps new content at 100 nodes a month, a limit a daily planner will meet quickly since each bullet counts. Pro costs $6.99 a month on an annual plan or $8.99 monthly, and Teams costs the same per user.

Data is stored on AWS in Northern Virginia, and the privacy policy (February 2026) names no certifications for Workflowy itself. AI chat, AI nodes and actions on Pro send content to OpenAI and Anthropic, which the AI terms say may not train on it. Exports to OPML and Markdown, Dropbox backup and a public API make leaving straightforward.

Summary

Workzone is an American project management service sold to marketing, creative and operations teams in universities, healthcare, banks and non-profits. Its distinguishing offer is people: onboarding, unlimited training and phone support are included in the price.

Projects are planned as task lists and Gantt charts with dependencies, alongside simpler card boards, a cross-workspace calendar, a personal to-do list and portfolio status reports. Intake request forms, document proofing with markups and approvals, timesheets and workload reports serve agency-style work. Custom fields and critical path arrive only on Enterprise.

There is no free plan and every tier is billed annually. Starter at $8 per user per month suits up to 25 users; Team at $20, with a five-user minimum, is where time tracking, intake and proofing begin. Enterprise is quote-based and charges only for core users, with five free collaborators each.

Data is processed in the United States with no region choice; Workzone states SOC 2 Type II and offers a HIPAA BAA on Enterprise. Its AI runs on an open-weight model inside its own environment and is not trained on customer data. Getting data out is the weak point: the API is a paid Enterprise feature.

Zenkit Projects

Zenkit Projects - summary, assessment and sources

Capabilities

TimeTime tracking: Not native.
BoardsKanban or Scrum boards: Native.
GanttGantt or dependency timeline: Native.
CalCalendar view: Native.
SyncTwo-way calendar sync: Native.

Summary

Zenkit Projects is a German work-management service in which every project is a list of items with typed fields that can be shown in eight ways. It suits small and mid-sized teams who want spreadsheet structure and project views in one place, with data kept in Germany.

The same list can appear as a table, Kanban board, plain list, calendar, Gantt chart, mind map, hierarchy or wiki. The Gantt supports dependencies and milestones; critical path, lag and other dependency types need Business. Automations, dashboards and portfolios sit on top. There is no time tracking.

There is no free plan, only a 14-day trial. Plus at $8 per seat (annual) caps the organisation at 10 users and 6 GB; Team at $12 removes the user cap and adds the iCal feed; Business at $21 adds the API, SAML SSO, SCIM and activity auditing. Quotas on items, comments and automation runs apply to every tier.

All data and backups are on AWS in Frankfurt, encrypted at rest, with a GDPR DPA on request; Zenkit cites AWS’s ISO 27001 rather than its own. AI features, priced on request, run in the EU and are not trained on customer data. Lists export to CSV or JSON, so leaving is practical list by list.

Assessment

Value for money2.8
No free plan; $8 Plus stops at 10 users, and API and SSO need Business at $21 a seat.
Ease of use3.6
Lists switch between eight views without setup, but fields, list types and hierarchies take time to learn.
Enterprise features3.4
SAML SSO, SCIM, activity audit and central user management on Business; no certification held by Zenkit itself.
Interface flexibility4.5
Table, Kanban, list, calendar, Gantt, mind map, hierarchy and wiki views with custom fields, automations, dashboards and forms.
Data control2.8
Every account sits on AWS in Frankfurt with an Article 28 DPA, but there is no region choice or own certification.
Portability3.8
Lists export to CSV or JSON with files as ZIP, Trello and Asana importers, but the API needs Business.

Record

First launched
2016. Public release of Zenkit in October 2016, per the vendor’s about page; work began at Axonic in 2014.
Vendor
Axonic GmbH, Karlsruhe, Germany (Amtsgericht Mannheim HRB 110424); privately held, managed by Martin Welker. Axonic also makes Zenkit To Do, Hypernotes, Zenforms and Zenchat.
Website
zenkit.com
Plans
Plus $8 per seat per month billed annually ($9 monthly), up to 10 users; Team $12 ($14); Business $21 ($25) with API, SSO, SCIM and activity audit; Enterprise quote-only. Prices cover Zenkit Projects only; Zenkit AI and Zenkit Flow are on request.
Free plan
No free plan on the current pricing page: a 14-day trial, after which an unpaid organisation is usually limited to data export and later deleted.
Hosting
AWS Frankfurt (RDS and S3, contracted through AWS Luxembourg), with encrypted daily backups in a separate Frankfurt data centre. No region choice and no on-premise edition documented.
Security
TLS 1.2+, AES-256 at rest, Argon2 password hashing, app-based 2FA on all plans; SAML SSO, SCIM, activity auditing and central user management on Business; certifications cited are AWS’s (ISO 27001, SSAE 16), not Zenkit’s; GDPR DPA available by email.
Calendar sync
Two-way Google Calendar sync per list, including creating and deleting entries (recurring tasks Zenkit to Google only); Outlook and Apple Calendar only through a one-way iCalendar subscription, which the pricing table places on Team and above.
Data out
Per-list export to CSV or JSON, files as a ZIP, and printing; importers for Trello, Asana, CSV, Excel, Google Sheets and Microsoft Access; REST API on Business and above. After a lapsed trial the organisation is usually limited to export before deletion.
Platforms
Web, iOS, Android, and desktop apps for Windows, macOS and Linux.
AI
Zenkit AI is sold on request; the vendor says AI runs in the EU, calls models statelessly, does not store inputs or train on customer data, and asks for approval before modifying actions.
Integrations
Built-in Google Calendar sync, Trello, Asana, Excel and Access importers and file-storage connectors; most other links (Slack, Teams, Toggl, Clockify) run through Zapier or Integrately. A REST API is on Business and above.
Market signal
The vendor publishes no current Zenkit user count (about page, read November 2026, cites only 5 million users for Axonic’s earlier products); the English blog’s last post is dated December 2024, while the German blog posts monthly through October 2026.
Caveat
The product is still sold and maintained: the pricing, terms and security pages were revised in October and November 2026, the German blog posts monthly and a Zenkit Processes workflow module appeared in late 2025. But the English blog has been silent since December 2024, no dated public changelog is readable, and the help centre still documents a Free plan the pricing page no longer offers, so confirm plan terms in the trial.
Confidence
Medium-high

Amazing Marvin - summary, assessment and sources

Capabilities

TimeTime tracking: Native.
BoardsKanban or Scrum boards: Native.
GanttGantt or dependency timeline: Not native.
CalCalendar view: Native.
SyncTwo-way calendar sync: Native.

Summary

Amazing Marvin is a personal task manager and day planner that a Swiss micro-company has run since 2017. It is sold to individuals who struggle with procrastination or ADHD and want to tune the tool to how their own head works.

Every feature is a ‘strategy’ you switch on or off: Kanban boards, a calendar with time blocking, time tracking, habits, goals, a task jar, reward points and procrastination prompts. The result can be a plain checklist or a dense personal system. There are no Gantt charts and no team workspaces; the only AI feature is a braindump sorter in the mobile apps.

There is one plan, Marvin Pro, at $12 a month or $96 a year, with a 14-day trial and no free tier. Students get half price and the vendor offers pay-what-you-can on request, which is unusual. The mobile apps were rebuilt in September 2026.

The privacy policy, last updated in January 2020, names Google App Engine and IBM Cloudant for storage, with US transfers; there are no certifications. Cloud sync can be turned off so data stays in the browser or desktop app. Backups export everything as JSON, and a documented API with webhooks and full database access makes leaving realistic.

Assessment

Value for money3.0
No free plan, and $8 a month annually or $12 monthly is high for a one-person tool, though everything is included.
Ease of use2.8
Over 100 features and 300 settings switched on one by one; productive quickly only once you choose a workflow.
Enterprise features1.0
A single-user tool by design: no admin console, no SSO, and only light task sharing and comments.
Interface flexibility3.8
Lists, Kanban, calendar, smart lists, custom screens and dozens of toggled strategies, plus API and webhooks; no custom fields.
Data control2.4
No certifications and a 2020 privacy policy naming US clouds, but cloud sync can be switched off to keep data local.
Portability3.8
Full JSON backup of tasks, projects and settings, a read-write API and many importers; no CSV export.

Record

First launched
2017. Public launch of the app, as the vendor’s About page records it (work on it began in 2014).
Vendor
Amazing GmbH, a Swiss company founded and run by Christina Willner. Privately held; the About page lists a team of three.
Website
amazingmarvin.com
Plans
One plan, Marvin Pro: $12 a month billed monthly or $96 a year ($8 a month) billed annually, with every feature included.
Free plan
No free plan: a 14-day trial without a card, after which data is kept but tasks cannot be added or completed until you subscribe.
Hosting
Account data on Google App Engine and task data on IBM Cloudant, with transfers to the USA per the privacy policy (last updated 19 January 2020). No region choice; cloud sync can be disabled to keep data on the device only.
Security
Account data encrypted in transit and at rest, task data in transit (the help centre makes no at-rest claim for tasks), and optional two-factor authentication. No SOC 2 or ISO 27001 claimed. No SSO, SCIM or audit log.
Calendar sync
Two-way sync with Google, iCloud, Yahoo and CalDAV calendars on the single plan; Outlook and Exchange sync is in beta, and public ICS feeds can be imported read-only.
Data out
Backup of all data (tasks, projects, labels, time blocks, settings, notebooks, habits) as compressed or plain JSON; automatic backups in the desktop app; REST API, webhooks and direct CouchDB access. Projects can be copied out as text; no CSV export.
Platforms
Web, macOS, Windows, Linux, iOS, Android, Apple Watch and a browser extension.
AI
AI Braindump in the iOS and Android apps rebuilt in September 2026: typed or spoken text is sorted into tasks and projects, not yet on the web. The vendor names no AI provider and the January 2020 privacy policy does not mention AI or training.
Integrations
Calendar sync (Google, iCloud, Yahoo, CalDAV, Outlook in beta), Zapier, email-to-Marvin, a browser extension, Siri and Alexa; importers for Todoist, TickTick, Things, OmniFocus and CSV. A REST API with webhooks and direct database access is documented.
Market signal
The homepage claims ‘5K+ happy users’ and the About page names three staff (both checked November 2026); no revenue or customer figures are published.
Caveat
The privacy policy has not been updated since January 2020, so its hosting and transfer statements may not reflect current practice, and it says nothing about the AI braindump added to the mobile apps in September 2026.
Confidence
Medium-high
