Fifty-seven products, compiled 10 November 2026. Expand a row for capabilities, scores and sources. Scores are editorial judgements on a 1-5 scale.

No product matches those filters

Native time tracking, Gantt, a calendar and two-way sync for one audience rules out nearly everything, and partial support never satisfies a must-have. Loosen one filter and try again.

    Market presence is an editorial band read from users, customers, revenue and headcount, not a market-share figure. Prices were read from vendor pricing pages around 10 November 2026, per user per month billed annually, in US dollars; ≈ marks a flat team price shown per person for ten people, or a converted currency; a † marks a price with a further qualification. Integration figures estimate packaged connectors and marketplace apps; APIs and webhooks are in each record.

    Where to start

    The matrix says what each product does and costs. These are the routes the research supports.

    A 50-5,000 person organisation that needs SSO, audit logs and a say over where the data lives
    Start with Asana, monday work management and Smartsheet. All three sell SAML, provisioning and audit logging on their enterprise tiers, Smartsheet partly as add-ons. Residency is where they differ: Asana sells it on Enterprise+, monday fixes the region from the first user’s location, and Smartsheet keeps separate EU and Australian regions.
    An organisation already paying for Microsoft 365
    Try Microsoft Planner before buying anything else. Basic Planner comes with the suites; Planner Plan 1 at $10 adds Gantt timelines, sprints and goals. Microsoft To Do keeps each person’s own list beside it.
    A software team running sprints, backlogs and releases
    Jira for configurable workflows and the largest marketplace; Linear for speed and an EU region on every plan. YouTrack is the cheapest here at $4.50, free up to ten users, and still sold as a server you run yourself. Azure Boards if the code already lives in Azure DevOps.
    Data that must stay in the EU, or on your own servers
    YouTrack, Azure Boards, Celoxis and Teamhood all offer an edition you can run on-premise; Bitrix24 does too, but read its record on jurisdiction first. For EU cloud hosting by default, MeisterTask runs in Frankfurt. If control is the deciding requirement, start with the open-source directory instead.
    A small team on a tight budget
    Zoho Projects at $4 a seat brings Gantt, timesheets and issue tracking. Freedcamp at $1.49 and Plaky at $3.99 are cheaper still. Trello’s free plan works until the eleventh collaborator.
    A team that thinks in boards
    Trello is still the reference board. MeisterTask adds native time tracking and German hosting; Favro lets the same cards sit on boards, sheets and roadmaps across teams. Businessmap for Kanban with WIP limits at department scale, from fifteen seats.
    One person, a to-do list and several devices
    Todoist for fast capture and dependable sync. TickTick if a calendar, habits and a focus timer belong in the same app. Microsoft To Do or Google Tasks if free matters more than features and the account already exists.
    Planning each day against a calendar
    Sunsama for a deliberate daily plan; Akiflow to pull tasks from many tools into one inbox first; Motion to let software place the tasks in the calendar for you. Tweek if a paper-like week is all you want.
    Documents, databases and tasks in the same place
    Notion is the default and the broadest. Coda (Superhuman Docs) if the documents should compute. Airtable for relational data that outgrew a spreadsheet, now owned by Bending Spoons. Fibery for product teams who want to model their own objects.
    An agency or studio billing client hours
    Productive ties tasks to budgets, resourcing and invoices; Teamwork.com is project management built around client work. Paymo for freelancers and small studios, from $5.90 for one person.
    A project manager who lives in Gantt charts
    GanttPRO for critical path and baselines from $8; TeamGantt for a flat account price and a gentler learning curve. Celoxis when the Gantt has to roll up into a portfolio with resource capacity.
    Client work on a flat bill, without counting seats
    Basecamp for to-dos, message boards and chat per project, with clients inside. ProofHub at $45 a month for unlimited users, if Gantt and proofing matter more than polish.

    How the scores work

    Six criteria, each 1 to 5, each with a written justification. Four are shared with the open-source directory; two change, because a service someone else runs raises different questions.

    Value for money
    What the free plan gives, what the tier most teams actually need costs per seat, seat minimums, and what is held back for the top tiers or sold as an add-on.
    Ease of use
    Interface clarity, learning curve, conceptual overhead and whether non-specialists can live in it.
    Enterprise features
    SSO and SCIM, permissions, audit logs, admin controls, compliance certifications, portfolio reporting and scale.
    Interface flexibility
    How many genuinely useful views exist, plus custom fields, automation, dashboards, filters and extension points.
    Data control
    Where the data lives and who decides: region choice, certifications, encryption key management, a self-managed edition, and what AI features do with your content.
    Portability
    Export formats and how complete they are, the public API, importers, and how realistically you could leave.

    The Score column is their unweighted mean. The directory opens by market presence, largest first. Each record also carries a Confidence value: High means pricing, features and data handling were verified on the vendor’s own current pages; Medium-high flags one remaining qualification; Medium means part of the record rests on secondary sources. Read the caveat and sources with the label.

    A product sold only by quote scores low on value for money by design: a price a reader cannot see cannot be judged good value. That pulls the mean of enterprise suites down, so read their other five criteria on their own.

    The two directories share a scale but not two of their criteria, so a commercial product and an open-source one are best compared on the four criteria they share, not on the mean.

    Who each product is built for

    The label follows the market the vendor sells to, not every use the product can be put to. Plenty of software teams run on a general team tool, and plenty of individuals live in one built for teams.

    Personal
    Sold to individuals first: one person’s tasks, priorities and days. Some allow sharing, but there is little or no team administration, which is why the enterprise score is low by design.
    Teams
    General work management for any team: projects, assignments and shared views, sold per seat to small companies and departments as much as to large organisations.
    Software
    Issue tracking and delivery for software teams: backlogs, sprints, releases and links to code. Other teams can use it, but it is built around engineering’s vocabulary.
    Enterprise
    Portfolio, resource and professional-services management sold mainly to large organisations, often through a sales conversation rather than a self-serve plan.

    Questions

    Why does a directory of open-source software list closed-source products?

    Most people choosing a task manager are weighing a commercial service, and the open-source options are easier to judge against the market they compete with. This page applies the same method to fifty-seven of those services. No vendor pays to be listed, and there are no affiliate links.

    Why do two criteria differ from the open-source page?

    Ease of deployment means little for a service someone else runs, so Value for money takes its place. Data sovereignty becomes Data control: without the source, the questions are where the data lives, which certifications back that up, whether a self-managed edition exists, and what AI features do with your content.

    How are the prices compared?

    The Paid from column is the cheapest paid plan per user per month, billed annually, in US dollars as published around 10 November 2026. Monthly billing almost always costs more; each record gives both where the vendor publishes both. A flat team price is shown as what each of ten people would pay, a price in euros is converted, and both carry a ≈ with the published price beneath; a dagger marks a seat minimum or another qualification. The cheapest plan is rarely the one a growing team ends up on, and the record says which tier the limits push you towards.

    Does a free plan mean free?

    It means a permanent tier with no time limit. Most cap seats, projects, storage, automations or history, and each record says where. A free trial is not a free plan, and the filter does not count one.

    Are all fifty-seven assessed to the same depth?

    No. Every record carries a Confidence value. Each product was researched from the vendor’s own pricing, documentation and trust pages, checked against the live pages by a second reader, then edited against the rest of the set so that a 4 means the same thing in every row. Where a fact rests on a secondary source, the record says so.

    How current is this?

    Compiled on 10 November 2026. Commercial prices and plans change several times a year, far more often than open-source licences do, so check the vendor’s own page before you buy. Each record’s caveat names what was changing when it was written.

    Corrections and additions

    If a record is wrong, send the correction with a source. Prices rise, features move between tiers, products are acquired or shut down; each correction is checked against the same criteria as everything else.

    What gets listed

    Three rules: closed source, sold as a service, and usable in a web browser. A desktop-only app does not qualify, however good it is; neither does a product that has stopped selling. Nobody pays to be listed.

    Revisions
